airbus.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is progressing on its technology clock. Entry into service remains planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies, the production system and certification have matured, and not before. We are preparing its industrial ramp-up with the same discipline.

We confirm three engine makers on the aircraft: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. That gives our customers choice and secures supply.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it remain protected.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain. That means securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths, and recruiting the engineers who will build the Airbus of the 2030s.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
Decision: plan A, the company default.
- ngsa: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037.
- ngsa_engine_code: 7, unchanged.
- rea350: hold.
- delay_tactics: none.

Grid: +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible). The plan is positive in both columns, carries no Board item and uses no override.

The team rule, step by step.

1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
- Cancel NGSA (every cancel row) is deleted under rule 7. It would be a reaction to Boeing with no failed case behind it: -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), with a $25.37B write-off.
- Both moves (on every row) are deleted. They break rule 4, since both counts as two moves, and they fail the integrity pillar because both contains a bottleneck. They also lose $0.47B against one move.
- Bottleneck in place of poaching is deleted on integrity. Toepfer and Wagner both fail it as more than a first claim on our own capacity.

2. Survivors of both colleagues' tests.
- Only plan A passes Toepfer's tests and Wagner's tests together.
- Plan B (one poaching move, +25.02 / +24.54) fails Toepfer's peak-cash test: $5.27B in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line, a binding soft veto. It also trips round-1 break point (d).
- Plan D (A350 Re-engine, +24.91 / +21.67) fails peak cash at $6.67B and fails robustness at -1.21 in S2.
- Plan E (+26.56 / +23.32) fails peak cash at $6.87B, and its A350 part is -1.22 in S2.
- Wagner passes poaching and passes the A350 Re-engine on capacity at the limit, but recommends hold.

3. Choice. The highest-grid survivor in my expected column, S1, is plan A. No tie-break is needed.

4. Overrides considered and declined.
- Poaching clears $1B over plan A in both columns (+1.65 / +1.66), so an override of Toepfer's cash test is arithmetically open. I decline it for five reasons:
  - The Board applies its own $5.2B line and has said it would veto, and I have no override against the Board.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board, and I do not set it aside.
  - Toepfer flags that three of its five spend years (2037-39) would run with no Airbus programme in development, which is the spirit of rule 5.
  - Nothing in my record shows me using or favouring such a lever.
  - The money cannot be spent inside the line while NGSA spends.
- The A350 Re-engine trails plan A by $1.21B in S2, so it fails both the override rule and the Board's override review.
- No override is used; the budget of one per game stays intact.

5. What discipline costs on the grid.
- S1: $3.19B below row E and $1.65B below row B.
- S2: $1.66B below row B.
- These are costs of the binding cash test, the integrity pillar and the Board's vetoes. They are not a doctrine premium.

6. Delay Tactics are now closed for the game. fps enters service in 2040, and the next round is 2045. No move was ordered in either round, and nothing is said in public.

7. Against what I am paid to protect.
- Five pillars: plan A adds nothing that tests safety, quality or integrity [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- Ramp: there is no new concurrency on the shared NGSA/A350 teams while NGSA industrialises. The A320 ring-fence holds [AX-0010, AX-0054].
- The Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA is kept whole on its technology clock, entering service two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Boeing's fps on the 10-year path moves nothing (rules 1, 2 and 7) [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225].
- Board: the defaults are what it would approve.

8. Engine code. I keep 7 on Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's. All three makers are ready by 2037, CFM backstops UltraFan NB (which has no margin), code 3 is avoided, and the code is not a veto ground.

9. Board-gate lines. There is no Board item. For the package:
- five pillars: pass;
- Toepfer: pass on every test, with peak $5.07B, headroom $0.13B, no break point triggered (phasing and the euro rate cannot be seen in the brief), +22.88 in the worst column, and returns fundable at the lower end of the policy with no equity raise;
- Wagner: pass on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield and NGSA readiness; supply crunch not applicable;
- grid: +23.37 / +22.88.

10. What I take to the Board outside the orders.
- Toepfer's flag that the per-share dividend in 2035-36 depends on FCF of about $5.9B or more. The payout is set each year inside the 30-50% policy on actual FCF.
- Wagner's watch item on P&W new-build engines for the A320neo.
- The 2045 staged case for the A350 Re-engine, which now needs a widebody engine ready by its entry into service as well as the A350F and Spirit confirmation.

frame.situation:
Round 2, decision year 2035.

Public record (bulletin):
- Boeing launched fps in 2030 on the 10-year path, entering service in 2040, with CFM (code 3). It calls 2040 "a planning date with headroom built in", will "certify before we build at rate", is not changing 737 rates, and is "not starting a second development alongside this one".
- NGSA launched in 2030 and is in development for entry into service in 2037. That is a three-year lead: 1 pp a year while we are alone, then a long-run split of 47/53 (Boeing/Airbus) under the rules.
- Engines: all three makers launched in 2030 on our code 7. CFM ducted and P&W GTF2 are ready in 2036; RR UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, our entry-into-service year itself. NGSA is set to fly CFM + PW + RR, and CFM backstops any late maker. CFM also launched the Embraer partnership (ready 2037) and the GEnx upgrade for 787 customers (in service since 2033). RR says it will make no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. P&W says the GTF fleet keeps first call on its parts and shops.
- No 787 Re-engine and no Boeing Rate Increase is on the record.
- Observed shares for 2026-34 are the status quo: 60% narrowbody, 41.2% widebody. The brief reports no safety, quality or supply problem, no engine slip and no inject.

Plan A passes. NGSA spends $5.07B in each of 2035 and 2036 ($10.15B left) and nil from 2037. Headroom is $0.13B. No round-1 break point was triggered: the bill stands at $35.52B and no Delay Tactics were ordered. The brief does not report phasing or the euro. Worst column: S2, +22.88. No Board item.

Plan B fails peak cash, binding. One poaching move adds $0.20B a year through 2039, so 2035-36 run at $5.27B, $0.07B over. At +1.65 / +1.66 an override is arithmetically open, but the Board's own line still vetoes it.

Plan D fails, binding: $6.67B a year, and -1.21 in S2. Rule 6 is met at two years. An override clears $1B only in S1.

Net cash from $13.4B in 2030. Base case ($5.87B free cash flow): -$0.5B at end-2036 holding €3.20, +$6.9B at 30% payout. Stress case ($5.23B): -$5.0B and +$2.4B. In 2035-36, €3.20 needs about $5.9B. No equity raise is needed. Rating thresholds are not in my record.

A350 Re-engine, 2045: $1.0B a year, no overlap.

Engine code: I defer to Wagner and expect 7.

tests.name: Safety and quality, all options (quality result; the Board accepts no override)

My record stops at the end-2025 technical issues under root-cause investigation [AX-0056] and the A320 quality reports [AX-0057]. Nothing since then is on the board. This result, the NGSA readiness result and the A320 ramp result should go to the Board's twice-yearly safety review together.

Both is two moves (rule 4) and contains a bottleneck. Grid: both is +24.55 / +24.07, which is -0.47 against one move in each column. The A350 Re-engine + both row is +26.08 / +22.84, -0.48 against plan E. Bottleneck alone has the same grid value as poaching (+25.02 / +24.54), so it buys nothing that poaching does not. Against the best plan that passes my tests (E at +26.56 in S1, B at +24.54 in S2), both is -2.01 / -0.47. No override applies to a pillar or a red line.

tests.name: Integrity and rules 4-5: one poaching move (plans B and E)

NGSA is in development through 2036 (entry into service 2037), so rule 5 is met. Cost: $1B, at $0.20B a year in 2035-39. Grid: +1.65 / +1.66 against plan A. My pass rests on the profile's reading. The move is covert under the rules, so it is a Board item and stays out of the public statement. Two questions are not my tests. tests.name: A320 ramp shield (A320-ramp result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment (70-75 a month by end-2027, stabilising at 75). On this board it passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem
tests.numbers:
The end-2027 date is eight years behind us. The board carries no monthly rate, so I have no quarterly rate figure for 2035 and give none. The board shows Airbus at 60.0% narrowbody share and 1,200 deliveries a year in every year 2026-34 (observed) and to 2036 (brief), with no ramp problem reported. The ring-fence stands: A320 staff and supplier slots are protected from NGSA. No option on the menu draws on A320 ramp staff. An A350 Re-engine draws on the shared NGSA/A350 teams, and a poaching move or our open hiring must be sized so it does not touch A320 staff.

P&W says 'the GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers'. That is a watch item for A320neo new-build engine deliveries while GTF2 is in development. It is a statement of priority, not a reported shortfall. Mitigation: CFM is the second source on the A320neo, and the quarterly ramp report tracks P&W new-build deliveries.

tests.name: Supply crunch (supply result; the Board accepts no override)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no supply problem and no inject. Plan A adds no concurrency. Plans D and E would add 2 overlap years and $1.2B of strain, which this test would block only under a reported crunch.

What to secure next for the NGSA ramp after entry into service, in my order of priority:
1. Engines: rate commitments from all three makers, with CFM as backstop, because an engine shortfall is what slipped the A320 ramp [AX-0054].
2. The rate-capable wing work packages [A-0441, AX-0060].
3. Titanium forgings [AX-0063, A-0457].
4. Rare earths [AX-0062].
All are sized to our own NGSA and A320 needs and never over-contracted to deny a rival capacity.

tests.name: Production readiness: NGSA entry into service 2037, and rule 1 (red line)
tests.threshold: Entry into service only once the technologies, the production system and the rate-capable wing are mature, with certification ahead of rate; no NGSA entry into service before 2035 (rule 1)
tests.numbers: The technology-ready year is 2035, and NGSA enters service in 2037, two years later, so rule 1 holds. No inject touches the technologies, the production system or the wing, so on the board they are on track. The board does not model the wing at rate or certification ahead of rate. I carry them as gates for the safety review, and in public we give a window ('the second half of the 2030s'), not dates. Engines against a 2037 entry into service: CFM ducted ready 2036 (1 year of margin), GTF2 2036 (1 year), UltraFan NB 2037 (no margin). This report should go to the Board's twice-yearly safety review with the A320 ramp report.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6: A350 Re-engine launched 2035 (plans D and E)

This would be the only launch this round (NGSA launched in round 1). NGSA develops over 2030-37 and the A350 Re-engine over 2035-40, so they overlap in 2035-36: 2 years. Strain is $3B x 2/5 = $1.2B ($0.6B a year). That is at the limit, with no slack. A one-year NGSA slip, which our own history says to assume, would make it 3 years and $1.8B, over the limit. Supply flag, not a veto ground and not priced on the board: no new widebody engine is on the record for the A350 Re-engine. RR says it makes no widebody engine spend without a Re-engine. An UltraFan WB launched in 2035 is ready in 2041 (6 years), one year after a 2040 entry into service.

My record stops in 2025: the A350F entering its industrial phase with the first two prototypes in final assembly [AX-0082], and the Spirit A350 packages acquired [AX-0060]. The brief carries no 2035 status for the A350F or Spirit, so I cannot confirm completion from data. Before a 2045 case I want both confirmed: the A350F in service and the Spirit A350 packages at rate.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. A reported supply crunch, A320 quality escape or ramp problem. I would fail any new concurrency (an A350 Re-engine, or a poaching move that draws on shared teams) and put the A320 first. NGSA would continue and would never be cancelled.
2. P&W's priority for its GTF fleet turning into A320neo engine delivery shortfalls. I would take it to the Board's safety review and lean on CFM as the second source. On NGSA I would still keep code 7, since a late or short maker is dropped at no cost. I would move to code 5 only if P&W's record threatened the NGSA ramp itself.
3. An NGSA engine slip. RR or P&W would be dropped and CFM backstops, so the 2037 entry into service holds. If CFM ducted slipped past 2037, NGSA would fly a LEAP derivative: I would re-test readiness, not cancel.
4. The A350 Re-engine in 2035. I would move from hold to support only with evidence that the NGSA teams are free before 2037, or a grid gain of at least $1B in both columns (today it is +1.54 / -1.21). I would also want a widebody engine on the record that is ready by a 2040 entry into service. Otherwise it waits for the 2045 round. There it needs 0 overlap and $0 strain, the A350F and Spirit absorption confirmed, an engine ready by the 2050 entry into service, and no 787 Re-engine (rule 3).
5. Poaching. I would fail it if it drew on A320 ramp staff, or if no programme were in development (rule 5). Setting aside the team's stricter condition, and the cash line, are not my calls.
ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived. Confidence: Very low.

I recommend plan A: NGSA hold, code 7, A350 hold, Delay Tactics none. It passes every operating test. Safety and quality: no open issue is reported on the A320, the A350 or NGSA. Ramp: the board has no monthly rate, so no quarterly figure. Airbus holds 60% and 1,200 narrowbodies a year through 2034, with no ramp or supply problem reported. Supply crunch: not applicable.

NGSA for 2037: technologies ready in 2035, entry into service two years later. CFM ducted and GTF2 are ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. No slip is on the record. Keep code 7: a late maker is dropped, CFM backstops and the 2037 date holds. P&W's first call for its GTF fleet is a watch item for A320neo engine deliveries, not a crunch. CFM is our second source there.

A350 Re-engine in 2035: capacity passes at the limit (2 overlap years, $1.2B strain). Absorption passes on the game proxy only. I do not veto it, but I recommend hold. One NGSA slip year would mean 3 overlap years and $1.8B. No new widebody engine is on the record: UltraFan WB launched now is ready in 2041, after a 2040 entry into service.

Delay Tactics: bottleneck and both fail on integrity, and both also breaks rule 4. Binding. Poaching passes my tests; cash and the stricter condition are for Thomas and Guillaume.

Cancel NGSA: no failed case, so rule 7 deletes it.

decision.public_statement:
Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do.

Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is progressing on its technology clock. Entry into service remains planned for the second half of the 2030s, once the technologies, the production system and certification have matured, and not before. We are preparing its industrial ramp-up with the same discipline.

We confirm three engine makers on the aircraft: CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. That gives our customers choice and secures supply.

The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle business. Its production continues in a disciplined and controlled way, and the people and suppliers who deliver it remain protected.

We continue to strengthen a more sovereign European supply chain. That means securing work packages and critical materials such as titanium and rare earths, and recruiting the engineers who will build the Airbus of the 2030s.

On the widebody side, the A350 family, including the A350F, remains our focus.

We fund this within our financial framework: disciplined investment in our future portfolio, and shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.

On trade, we keep working with industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic for a zero-for-zero tariff regime in civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
Decision: plan A, the company default.
- ngsa: hold. NGSA continues to entry into service in 2037.
- ngsa_engine_code: 7, unchanged.
- rea350: hold.
- delay_tactics: none.

Grid: +23.37 in S1 (expected) and +22.88 in S2 (worst plausible). The plan is positive in both columns, carries no Board item and uses no override.

The team rule, step by step.

1. Delete red-line and pillar breaches.
- Cancel NGSA (every cancel row) is deleted under rule 7. It would be a reaction to Boeing with no failed case behind it: -39.65 against continuing in both columns (-39.09 / -39.08 on the A350 Re-engine rows), with a $25.37B write-off.
- Both moves (on every row) are deleted. They break rule 4, since both counts as two moves, and they fail the integrity pillar because both contains a bottleneck. They also lose $0.47B against one move.
- Bottleneck in place of poaching is deleted on integrity. Toepfer and Wagner both fail it as more than a first claim on our own capacity.

2. Survivors of both colleagues' tests.
- Only plan A passes Toepfer's tests and Wagner's tests together.
- Plan B (one poaching move, +25.02 / +24.54) fails Toepfer's peak-cash test: $5.27B in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line, a binding soft veto. It also trips round-1 break point (d).
- Plan D (A350 Re-engine, +24.91 / +21.67) fails peak cash at $6.67B and fails robustness at -1.21 in S2.
- Plan E (+26.56 / +23.32) fails peak cash at $6.87B, and its A350 part is -1.22 in S2.
- Wagner passes poaching and passes the A350 Re-engine on capacity at the limit, but recommends hold.

3. Choice. The highest-grid survivor in my expected column, S1, is plan A. No tie-break is needed.

4. Overrides considered and declined.
- Poaching clears $1B over plan A in both columns (+1.65 / +1.66), so an override of Toepfer's cash test is arithmetically open. I decline it for five reasons:
  - The Board applies its own $5.2B line and has said it would veto, and I have no override against the Board.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met on this board, and I do not set it aside.
  - Toepfer flags that three of its five spend years (2037-39) would run with no Airbus programme in development, which is the spirit of rule 5.
  - Nothing in my record shows me using or favouring such a lever.
  - The money cannot be spent inside the line while NGSA spends.
- The A350 Re-engine trails plan A by $1.21B in S2, so it fails both the override rule and the Board's override review.
- No override is used; the budget of one per game stays intact.

5. What discipline costs on the grid.
- S1: $3.19B below row E and $1.65B below row B.
- S2: $1.66B below row B.

boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane on a ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. I'll tell you plainly where it stands. The program is on its plan. 2040 is still our date. It's a planning date with headroom in it, not a stretch target. We're in the heavy years now: detailed design, building the test airplanes, and certification ahead of us. That's where programs get into trouble, so that's where we're being most careful. If anything moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

We're not changing anything else today. We're not starting a second development alongside this one. The 787 is a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service. Doing less and doing it better is what got us here, and it's what will get this airplane across the line.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our supply chain funded and healthy, and we'll keep our engineering teams together through entry into service and the ramp after it. Our engine partner stays CFM. We're funding this from our operations and our debt capacity, with no new equity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

There will be a few years when our customers see a newer airplane flying before ours. We've planned for that. We'll keep earning their business on the 737 MAX the old-fashioned way, by delivering what we promised, when we promised it.

Others will make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. This is the part of the climb where you keep your hands steady and do the work. The financials will follow our production performance, and we've got a lot of work in front of us.
boeing.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 2 (2035), under the team rule of teams.md §9. I propose and decide. Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can each block me.

1. Vetoes and flags in force.
- Malave holds a binding veto on both cancel rows, and I accept it.
  - C (cancel + 787 hold) scores -18.33 in S3, 15.55 below the -2.78 floor.
  - D (cancel + Re-engine) scores -16.66, 13.88 below the floor.
  - Neither row is in the orders.
- B (fps hold + Re-engine) passes his slip leg at S3 -0.13, 2.65 above the floor. His hold on B is advice, not a veto.
- Pope checked her KPI veto and did not invoke it. The rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live problem.
- Her flags are both correct, so I confirm them and strike the rows:
  - H4 on B: 5 years of overlap against a 2-year limit.
  - H5 on C and D.
- No flag is mistaken and nothing needs a rebuttal, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and deliveries were flat at 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies over 2026-34. Pope rightly says the board carries deliveries, not KPI data. So the KPI record comes directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- Are market, technology and balance sheet ready for a second development? No.
  - Market: the Re-engine's item is +0.65 in S1, inside ε, and -2.99 in S2.
  - Balance sheet: Malave finds the Re-engine not fundable from operations. On his curve it adds $7.69B of borrowing above operating profit over 2035-39 ($2.26B on an even spread), and he would not support investment grade with a second bill in the fps peak years [BX-1305].
  - The fps is the development in hand. We finish it first [B-2326].
- What if certification takes longer? I read S3 first. Do Nothing scores -0.78 there, 2.00 above the floor. Malave's quarterly check finds no evidence that the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong [BX-1319], so there is no reset to make, and I will not make one for the sake of it. One reset, if it comes, made early [BX-1318].
- Is this doing less, better? A and B are within ε in S1 (+0.66 against +1.31) and in S3 (-0.78 against -0.13). A leads by 2.99 in S2. Doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] both give it to A. Malave's worst-column rule picks A by 2.99.

3. Rulings on the hard rules.
- H1 is not at issue; the fps is launched.
- H2 cannot bind.
- H3:
  - First half: it lapsed after 2030. Its re-founded ground, one development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], now works through H4.
  - Second half: not triggered, since the public record shows no A350 Re-engine. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars ours from 2045, and I accept that.
- H4 binds. The fps counts 2033-40 and a 2035 Re-engine 2035-40: 5 years against 2. re787 stays at hold.
  - Hard-rule cost: 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2, where holding saves 2.99. Logged apart from any premium.
  - Earliest window: the 2045 round (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap).
- H5 binds. The fps stays whole.
  - Keeping it beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55, so H5 forgoes nothing.
  - A cancel would write off $30.16B in 2035 with the penalty staying.
- H6 is not in play.
- H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- H8: premium 0 this round. Cumulative 0.46 (Round 1), within the $2B cap.

4. Debt and funding, Malave's figures, adopted as the Finance Committee baseline.
- Do Nothing carries -4.73 of debt penalty already netted ($19.1B undiscounted for scale). It is never subtracted again.
- On his planning curve:
  - spend peaks in 2036 at about $8.44B, $1.74B above operating profit;
  - 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B of room built in 2030-34;
  - 2039 turns positive, and the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt.
- That is fundable within investment grade with no new equity, on the fps alone.
- His curve is an inference, because the brief gives no phasing. I have asked him to replace it with programme actuals each quarter. His triggers go to the Board before anything is committed.

5. Engine code: 3 (CFM). This is the last code decision before EIS.
- CFM ducted is ready in 2036, with the LEAP derivative as a floor.
- Code 3 against NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair.
- I considered a second source (5, 6 or 7): GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so all qualify by date. I rejected it:
  - none of these engines is in service today, and about three years on NGSA by 2040 is short of durability shown [BX-1298];
  - it would add a second propulsion integration and certification inside the fps's heaviest years, the same capacity ground as H4;
  - Pope cannot show it adds supply security on matured, durable engines.
- CFM's load across both airframers is real [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We manage it with allocation tracking and contracted delivery commitments.
- My confidence on engine choice is Low, so doctrine plus Pope's test drove this.

6. Expected scenario: S1, provisional; my confidence on Airbus is Low. My Round-1 read of an A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA did not happen. A move is real only when it is launched. The orders are the same in every column, so the read does not drive the decision.

7. Doctrine and record. Several of these calls rest on company doctrine, not my own record: H4, H5, the code-3 default and the 2044 hedge window. Others are my record: one development at a time, debt first, never walk away from a core programme, reset once, no fixed-price development and certify before rate.

8. The Board. All four orders are holds, which matches its would-approve list, so no item goes to review. Its seven recommendations are answered in board_response.

9. What would change this:
- a finding that the estimate or date is wrong: we reset once, now, costed in full and brought to the Board;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;

frame.question:
2035 is a round for carrying what we started, not for starting something new. The fps is five years into a ten-year plan. The brief shows it on its 2040 date, with no slip and no certification trouble, and no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. So the question is narrow. Does anything earn a place beside the fps this round: a 787 Re-engine, a cancel or an engine-code change? And does our 2040 date still carry the headroom we said it had?

I'm putting my four questions to this ExCo.
(1) Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live problem, and I want Pope's seat to confirm it on the record for the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259].
(2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet ready for a second development while the fps is in its heaviest years [BX-1296, BX-1305]?
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave to read the risk-case column S3 before anything else, and to tell me whether anything shows our fps estimate is wrong [BX-1319].
(4) Is each plan doing less, better? I want every row set against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

**Where we are (bulletin and brief).**
- Round 1 was adjudicated. Our fps launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp, with EIS 2040 and CFM selected. Airbus launched NGSA in 2030, with EIS 2037 and code 7 (RR, PW and CFM). No A350 Re-engine has been launched.

**Do Nothing** (fps continues, 787 hold, rate hold) scores +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 (S1 rivals hold / S2 A350 Re-engine / S3 risk case, Airbus Delay Tactics). Its components:
- narrowbody operating profit +20.30;
- programme investment -14.91, booked at EIS;
- debt penalty -4.73, already netted, never subtracted again. For scale only, the undiscounted penalty on the 10-year fps is $19.1B.

**Incumbency path.** Narrowbody share runs 39 / 38 / 37% in 2037-39 while NGSA is alone, then 38% in 2040, back to 40% in 2042 and 47% by 2049. That is a 47/53 long-run split for a 3-year NGSA lead. Both objectives (50/50 and incumbency) are recorded as not met, and no order offered this round changes that. So no objective premium applies.

**Funding.** Airplane operating profit is 6.7 through 2036, then 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39. Against about $6.03B a year of even-spread fps spend (inference), cover rises from 90% to 91 / 93 / 94%, and the cushion shrinks from $0.67B to $0.57B / $0.47B / $0.37B a year.

**Grid against Do Nothing** (S1 / S2 / S3; S3 floor -2.78):
- 787 Re-engine with the fps: row +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13; item +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65.
  - Launched now, it enters service in 2040. The board's strain counts it 2035-40 against the fps's 2033-40: 5 years of overlap and $3.0B of strain undiscounted, already netted.

  - Real spend of about $1.0B a year over 2035-39 takes total spend to about $7.03B a year. That is 105-110% of operating profit, about $2.25B borrowed above it over five years.
- Cancel the fps: row -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33; item -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. The write-off is $30.16B in 2035 (60.32 × 5/10), and the penalty stays.
- Cancel with a Re-engine: row -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66; item -17.32 / -20.96 / -15.88. The Re-engine item beside a cancel is +1.67 / -1.97 / +1.67.

**Board risks** (from its guidance; these are not my red lines). It would veto:

- re787: launch with the fps on hold, for three reasons: it never clears $1B in any column; it is -2.99 in S2, which the bulletin does not rule out; and it carries 5 years of overlap against its 2-year limit;

It would approve Do Nothing, and code 3 or any code whose makers are ready by 2040. If every order is a hold, it is not called to review, and its recommendations carry into 2045.

Risk case: Do Nothing is +0.66 in S1 and -0.78 in S3. The $1.44B swing is 218% of the S1 value, so the plan's whole positive value rides on a clean ramp around EIS. Sensitivity: S3 is 5 pp for 5 years from EIS (2040-44), i.e. 100 aircraft a year at about $14.1M each (fps $55M at 25.64%): $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B PV. Each pp-year around EIS costs about $0.28B nominal ($0.06B PV). S3 floor -2.78: A -0.78 passes by 2.00; B -0.13 passes by 2.65; C -18.33 fails by 15.55; D -16.66 fails by 13.88. Headroom: the board carries no design-maturity, test or certification data and no Boeing slip. I can confirm the date on the board, not the margin inside it; the Chief Engineer must show that to Aerospace Safety. Early warning: 2035 is the last ExCo round before EIS (the next is 2045), so my watch items go on the record now: (1) CFM ducted ready 2036, four years before EIS; (2) supplier and staff readiness for 2040-44; (3) the funding cushion falling to $0.37B in 2039.

tests.name: Two-front strain (engineering capacity), row B: 787 Re-engine launched in 2035 (doctrine; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and a 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5. The fps counts from EIS-7 to EIS, the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers: The fps 10-year counts 2033-40. A Re-engine launched in 2035 enters service in 2040 and counts 2035-40. Overlap is 5 years and strain $3.0B undiscounted, already netted in the grid and not to be subtracted again. It fails H4 by 3 years. I confirm H4 and do not rebut it: we do not have the engineering capacity for a second development in the fps's heaviest design, test and certification years. One development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393]. Row A (recommended): 0 years, $0. Earliest legal window: a 2045 launch (EIS 2050, counting 2045-50) has 0 years of overlap, and only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half).

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers: No ramp order is offered. The fps is launched on the 10-year ramp: EIS 2040, $60.32B at EIS, strain 0 standing alone. A re-baseline is a plan and a statement, not an order. Round 1 chose the 10-year ramp because its nominal date matched where doctrine's central three-year clean-sheet slip would put a 7-year ramp.

tests.name: Supplier and talent readiness, the hedge against S3 (doctrine; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: No live supply-chain or workforce problem. Fragile suppliers funded and kept hot above our rate. Engineering staff held through the risk window. Exposure assessed with no attribution.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no live supply-chain problem and names no fragile supplier, so I name categories, not companies. The S3 window is 2040-44 (5 years from EIS), so the hedge runs through 2044, not only 2040. Keep hot and funded above our rate [B-2330, BX-1243]: the fps's long-lead airframe structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth-dependent parts and the CFM engine line. Embed staff wherever a supplier falls behind [B-2097]. Talent: hold the fps engineering and certification teams through 2044 and assign none to a second development. Answer scarcity by transfer, hiring and retention, as before [B-0729, B-1941, B-1376]; engineering talent is a competition with every sector [B-1835]. Exposure: the public long-term agreements on engines, wing packages, titanium and rare earths, and the European engineering hiring, are ordinary market moves. Our exposure is to shared, finite capacity in titanium forgings, rare earths and engines during the 2040-44 ramp, when NGSA (EIS 2037) is already in service. Mitigation: long-term agreements sized to our own 2040 plan, on our own schedule. The cost of failure is $1.41B a year nominal (S3).

tests.name: Engine code and supply security (doctrine; not a payoff item; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Request only makers with a new NB engine ready by EIS 2040, matured, with durability shown before EIS [BX-1298]. Weigh each maker's capacity across both airframers and the aftermarket [BX-1264, BX-1325].
tests.numbers: Ready dates: CFM ducted 2036, GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037, all before 2040. Code 4: no Joint Venture has formed, and one formed in 2035 is ready in 2041, after EIS, so the request would fall back to CFM. This is our last code decision: the code can change only until EIS, and the next round is 2045. Code 3: CFM is always available, as a LEAP derivative if ducted falls short. That puts a floor on the board under the sole-source pacing risk seen on the GE9X [B-1597]. Doctrine is sole source by default, chosen for maturity [B-0600, B-0613]. Second source (5, 6, 7): in 2035 none of the new engines is in service. By 2040, GTF2 and UltraFan NB would have about 3 years on NGSA, as would CFM ducted. Durability problems on the newer engines appeared in service [BX-1298, B-2304], so 3 years falls short of durability shown. A second engine also adds a second propulsion integration and certification in 2035-40, inside the fps's heaviest years (inference: the same capacity ground as H4). The supply-security risk is real: CFM supports NGSA, the A320neo, the 737 aftermarket and the fps [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Mitigation: track engine allocation by airframer, which is easy to measure [B-1923], and contract delivery commitments. Code 3 passes. I cannot show that a second source adds security on matured, durable engines.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Invest Solo where Boeing owns the IP. Partner where it can't, and only where the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: The fps airframe is Solo, and its IP is Boeing's. No partner order is offered this round. The engine is where Boeing owns no IP, so we partner with an engine maker either way; the test there is what a second partner adds (engine test above). A cancel would write off $30.16B of IP investment in 2035 (60.32 x 5/10), and the penalty would stay.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase and Charleston (inference from [BX-1329]; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Back added capacity only where the grid shows visible demand for it in the expected column.
tests.numbers: rate_737 is offered only at hold. Widebody: without a Re-engine, the board holds Boeing at 100 WB a year (58.8% of 170) from 2026 to 2060. That is about 8.3 a month, below the 10 a month that the Charleston expansion is built to exceed [B-2336, BX-1317]. Charleston can carry the 787 to the 2045 window without a Re-engine. The board shows no demand above 100 a year for extra capacity to meet, so growth beyond that is a commercial move and unpriced.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number with a sensitivity per unit of change.
tests.numbers: A: the fps's $60.32B is booked at EIS 2040, an even spread of $6.03B a year (inference; Malave owns the real phasing). Over 2035-39 that is $30.16B against $32.9B of operating profit (6.7, 6.7, 6.6, 6.5, 6.4). Cover is 90/90/91/93/94%, and the cushion is $0.67/0.67/0.57/0.47/0.37B a year, $2.74B in all. That absorbs a 9.1% overrun on the remaining spend before we borrow. B: +$5B at 2040, about $1.0B a year. Spend rises to $7.03B a year, cover to 105-110%, and $2.26B is borrowed above operating profit over 2035-39. Undiscounted debt penalty (alpha 0.30, debt $45B, EV $130B): the fps alone carries $19.1B. The Re-engine beside it adds $3.10B ($0.62B per $1B), against $0.60B alone ($0.12B per $1B), so the marginal cost is five times higher. Penalty and strain are already netted in the grid. C: $30.16B written off in 2035, and the penalty stays; item -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. D: item -17.32 / -20.96 / -15.88. A converts cash best. Malave's veto decides the slip leg.

tests.name: Customers through the gap (record [BX-1331], applied by inference; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: No order offered this round changes the 2037-40 share path. Hold the base by delivering the 737 on time and predictably, and quantify the gap.
tests.numbers: Brief: NB share 39/38/37% in 2037-39 and 38% in 2040, back to 40% in 2042 and 47% by 2049. The dip costs $0.1/0.2/0.3B of operating profit in 2037-39, $0.6B nominal. ops.would_change_mind_if: Four things would change my view. (1) A brief or a Chief Engineer report showing a live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem. I would invoke the binding KPI veto on any Rate Increase and ask for the fps date to be reset once, now. (2) Evidence that 2040 has lost its headroom: design maturity, testing or certification authorisation behind plan, or CFM ducted slipping past 2036. Then we reset once and early, costed in full: concessions, rework, learning curve and carrying cost. (3) Evidence now of CFM allocation or delivery trouble across the two airframers, together with a GTF2 test record showing time on wing and full-life parts proven. I would then back code 6 as a supply hedge, since this is the last code round before EIS. (4) For the Re-engine: in the 2045 round, with the fps in service and no A350 Re-engine, the overlap is 0 years and my strain test passes.
ops.memo:
My record is thin: two Global Services events, nothing from BCA. Delivery, cash and IP are my record, applied to airplanes by inference; the KPI, supplier and strain tests are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time, predictable delivery. The brief shows the fps on its 2040 date, no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies a year. The KPI gate passes; my veto is not in play. The risk case is the number to manage: 5 points of share for 5 years from EIS costs $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B in present value. Each point earns $0.28B a year on the fps against $0.08B on the 737. So fragile suppliers stay funded and engineers stay in place through 2044, not just 2040.

Second, engineering capacity. A Re-engine now runs 2035-40 against the fps's 2033-40: 5 years of overlap and $3.0B of strain, against a 2-year limit. One development at a time. Its window is 2045.

Third, cash. Over 2035-39 the fps takes $30.16B of $32.9B operating profit. The $2.74B cushion covers a 9% overrun. The Re-engine turns it into $2.26B borrowed, and beside the fps each $1B adds about $0.62B of penalty, against $0.12B alone.

And finally, engines. This is our last code decision before EIS. Code 3: CFM always has its LEAP fallback, and a second engine is a second integration in our heaviest certification years, with no new engine yet in service.

Orders: fps hold, code 3, rate hold, Re-engine hold.

other_moves.move: Hold 2040 as a planning date with headroom; reset once and early
other_moves.detail: Restate EIS 2040 as a planning baseline with buffer in it, not a stretch target. Keep any earlier internal date back as upside and never publish it. If design maturity, test, certification or the CFM ducted engine (ready 2036) move the date, report it early with the mitigation attached, cost it once and in full (concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost), and bring it to the Board before the 2045 round if need be [B-2315, BX-1318, BX-1306, B-2349]. For scale only (Malave): each year of slip costs about $1.9B PV, plus 1 pp of long-run share for good.

other_moves.detail: No production-certification concurrency in the fps plan [BX-1263, B-2228]. The Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer report 737, 787 and fps KPI, supplier and certification results directly to the Aerospace Safety Committee every year. The board carries deliveries only, so those results, not delivery counts, are the KPI record [BX-1271, BG-0043]. Public as a commitment; the reports themselves are internal.

other_moves.move: No fixed-price development; risk-sharing supplier terms continue
other_moves.detail: fps development stays on cost-plus or back-to-back terms with suppliers and the engine maker [BX-1262, BX-1304]. Not priced on the board.

other_moves.move: Yearly funding report to the Finance Committee: fund from operations and debt capacity, no new equity
other_moves.detail: Malave's planning curve is the baseline until programme actuals replace it each quarter: fps spend 7.24 / 8.44 / 7.84 / 6.64 / 5.43 in 2035-39 against operating profit 6.7 / 6.7 / 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4. Peak 2036 at about $8.4B, $1.74B above operating profit; 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B room built in 2030-34; 2039 turns positive; the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt. Investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity and debt the first call on free cash [BX-1305, BX-0556, B-2327]. Triggers back to the Board before commitment: operating profit below 6.6 / 6.5 / 6.4 in 2037-39, peak spend above about $8.4B, 2035-38 borrowing above the 2030-34 room, or any threat to the rating.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, and engineering teams in place, through 2044
other_moves.detail: Our hedge against the risk case S3 (5 pp for 5 years from EIS, $1.41B a year nominal, $1.44B PV). The window runs 2040-44, so the hedge runs through 2044, not 2040. Keep the fps long-lead airframe structures, titanium forgings, rare-earth-dependent parts and the CFM engine line funded above our rate; embed staff where a supplier falls behind; requalify or acquire if needed [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2097]. Long-term supply agreements sized to our own 2040 plan, on our own schedule. Hold the fps engineering and certification teams through 2044; retention and hiring as needed; none assigned to a second development. Others' supply agreements and hiring are ordinary market moves; we attribute nothing to anyone before exposure.

Code 3 beside NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair. Require a matured engine with durability proven on the ground before EIS [BX-1298]. Track CFM engine allocation by airframer and contract delivery commitments, because CFM supports NGSA, the A320neo, the 737 aftermarket and the fps [BX-1264, BX-1325].

Any finding is reported a year ahead, not at the gate [BX-1306].

Until then the 787 grows from Charleston capacity [BX-1317, B-2336]. The board holds Boeing at 100 widebodies a year, so that growth is commercial and unpriced.

Deliver the 737 MAX on the dates promised; quote fps slots only against the 2040 planning date, never an earlier internal date; make every transaction trust-building [BX-1273, B-2315]. Pricing is decided campaign by campaign. Not priced on the board.

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago we launched a new single-aisle airplane on a ten-year path, with entry into service in 2040. I'll tell you plainly where it stands. The program is on its plan. 2040 is still our date. It's a planning date with headroom in it, not a stretch target. We're in the heavy years now: detailed design, building the test airplanes, and certification ahead of us. That's where programs get into trouble, so that's where we're being most careful. If anything moves, you'll hear it from us early, with the plan to fix it, and we'll reset once.

We're not changing anything else today. We're not starting a second development alongside this one. The 787 is a strong airplane, and it has room to grow from our Charleston capacity. We'll look at its next step once this airplane is in service. Doing less and doing it better is what got us here, and it's what will get this airplane across the line.

A few things haven't changed. We'll certify before we build at rate. We won't take on fixed-price development. We'll keep our supply chain funded and healthy, and we'll keep our engineering teams together through entry into service and the ramp after it. Our engine partner stays CFM. We're funding this from our operations and our debt capacity, with no new equity. Paying down debt stays our priority, and we intend to stay solidly investment grade.

There will be a few years when our customers see a newer airplane flying before ours. We've planned for that. We'll keep earning their business on the 737 MAX the old-fashioned way, by delivering what we promised, when we promised it.

Others will make their plans on their own clock. Ours rests on our own readiness. This is the part of the climb where you keep your hands steady and do the work. The financials will follow our production performance, and we've got a lot of work in front of us.
decision.rationale:
ExCo deliberation, Round 2 (2035), under the team rule of teams.md §9. I propose and decide. Malave's buffer test and the KPI doctrine can each block me.

1. Vetoes and flags in force.
- Malave holds a binding veto on both cancel rows, and I accept it.
  - C (cancel + 787 hold) scores -18.33 in S3, 15.55 below the -2.78 floor.
  - D (cancel + Re-engine) scores -16.66, 13.88 below the floor.
  - Neither row is in the orders.
- B (fps hold + Re-engine) passes his slip leg at S3 -0.13, 2.65 above the floor. His hold on B is advice, not a veto.
- Pope checked her KPI veto and did not invoke it. The rate is offered only at hold, and the brief reports no live problem.
- Her flags are both correct, so I confirm them and strike the rows:
  - H4 on B: 5 years of overlap against a 2-year limit.
  - H5 on C and D.
- No flag is mistaken and nothing needs a rebuttal, so overrides is empty.

2. My four questions.
- Are the KPIs stable? The brief reports no live quality, FAA, certification or supply-chain problem, and deliveries were flat at 800 narrowbodies and 100 widebodies over 2026-34. Pope rightly says the board carries deliveries, not KPI data. So the KPI record comes directly from the Chief Engineer and the Chief Aerospace Safety Officer to the Aerospace Safety Committee [BX-1271, BX-1259].
- Are market, technology and balance sheet ready for a second development? No.
  - Market: the Re-engine's item is +0.65 in S1, inside ε, and -2.99 in S2.
  - Balance sheet: Malave finds the Re-engine not fundable from operations. On his curve it adds $7.69B of borrowing above operating profit over 2035-39 ($2.26B on an even spread), and he would not support investment grade with a second bill in the fps peak years [BX-1305].
  - The fps is the development in hand. We finish it first [B-2326].
- What if certification takes longer? I read S3 first. Do Nothing scores -0.78 there, 2.00 above the floor. Malave's quarterly check finds no evidence that the $60.32B or the 2040 date is wrong [BX-1319], so there is no reset to make, and I will not make one for the sake of it. One reset, if it comes, made early [BX-1318].
- Is this doing less, better? A and B are within ε in S1 (+0.66 against +1.31) and in S3 (-0.78 against -0.13). A leads by 2.99 in S2. Doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] both give it to A. Malave's worst-column rule picks A by 2.99.

3. Rulings on the hard rules.
- H1 is not at issue; the fps is launched.
- H2 cannot bind.
- H3:
  - First half: it lapsed after 2030. Its re-founded ground, one development at a time [B-0341, B-1526, B-1393], now works through H4.
  - Second half: not triggered, since the public record shows no A350 Re-engine. If Airbus launches one this round, it bars ours from 2045, and I accept that.
- H4 binds. The fps counts 2033-40 and a 2035 Re-engine 2035-40: 5 years against 2. re787 stays at hold.
  - Hard-rule cost: 0.65 in S1 and S3, nil in S2, where holding saves 2.99. Logged apart from any premium.
  - Earliest window: the 2045 round (EIS 2050, 0 years of overlap).
- H5 binds. The fps stays whole.
  - Keeping it beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55, so H5 forgoes nothing.
  - A cancel would write off $30.16B in 2035 with the penalty staying.
- H6 is not in play.
- H7 has no trigger; my FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- H8: premium 0 this round. Cumulative 0.46 (Round 1), within the $2B cap.

4. Debt and funding, Malave's figures, adopted as the Finance Committee baseline.
- Do Nothing carries -4.73 of debt penalty already netted ($19.1B undiscounted for scale). It is never subtracted again.
- On his planning curve:
  - spend peaks in 2036 at about $8.44B, $1.74B above operating profit;
  - 2035-38 draw $3.66B against the $8.77B of room built in 2030-34;
  - 2039 turns positive, and the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt.
- That is fundable within investment grade with no new equity, on the fps alone.
- His curve is an inference, because the brief gives no phasing. I have asked him to replace it with programme actuals each quarter. His triggers go to the Board before anything is committed.

5. Engine code: 3 (CFM). This is the last code decision before EIS.
- CFM ducted is ready in 2036, with the LEAP derivative as a floor.
- Code 3 against NGSA's code 7 is no forbidden pair.
- I considered a second source (5, 6 or 7): GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, so all qualify by date. I rejected it:
  - none of these engines is in service today, and about three years on NGSA by 2040 is short of durability shown [BX-1298];
  - it would add a second propulsion integration and certification inside the fps's heaviest years, the same capacity ground as H4;
  - Pope cannot show it adds supply security on matured, durable engines.
- CFM's load across both airframers is real [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We manage it with allocation tracking and contracted delivery commitments.
- My confidence on engine choice is Low, so doctrine plus Pope's test drove this.

6. Expected scenario: S1, provisional; my confidence on Airbus is Low. My Round-1 read of an A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA did not happen. A move is real only when it is launched. The orders are the same in every column, so the read does not drive the decision.

7. Doctrine and record. Several of these calls rest on company doctrine, not my own record: H4, H5, the code-3 default and the 2044 hedge window. Others are my record: one development at a time, debt first, never walk away from a core programme, reset once, no fixed-price development and certify before rate.

8. The Board. All four orders are holds, which matches its would-approve list, so no item goes to review. Its seven recommendations are answered in board_response.

9. What would change this:
- a finding that the estimate or date is wrong: we reset once, now, costed in full and brought to the Board;
- a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem;
- an A350 Re-engine, which closes our 2045 Re-engine window under H3.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed as my independent check on the estimate [BX-1316]. His veto binds only on the slip leg. It is a thin seat: his record is one call (Low), and his phasing curve is his own inference because the brief gives no phasing.

Taken in full:
- Buffer results: A is 2.00 above the floor, B 2.65 above, C 15.55 below and D 13.88 below. I accept his binding veto on C and D.
- Debt penalty: Do Nothing's -4.73 is confirmed. B would add $3.10B undiscounted (0.765 PV) against $0.60B for the Re-engine alone. B's strain is $3.0B. Both are netted already and never subtracted again.
- Cancel arithmetic: $30.16B written off, and keeping beats cancelling by 18.99 / 18.99 / 17.55.
- His finding that the estimate is not wrong, so there is no reset.
- The premium log.

Taken as advice:
- Hold on B. It agrees with my H4 strike, so it is not decisive.
- The worst-column rule. It agrees with A by 2.99.

His funding report becomes the Finance Committee baseline:
- peak in 2036 at about $8.44B;
- $3.66B drawn over 2035-38 against $8.77B built over 2030-34;
- the decade ends about $6.1B down on debt;
- investment grade supported on the fps alone, with no new equity.
I treat his curve as a plan, not a fact, until programme actuals replace it.

Taken in full:

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: two new single-aisle airplanes are launched, and there is a CFM engine on both today. We don't take that for granted. We don't have a birthright on any order, so we earn it the way we always have, by delivering. That starts with the LEAP engines and the spares our customers need right now, on time. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

The new ducted engine that CFM and our partners at Safran launched five years ago stays on its gate: not before 2036. We report against that gate on test, not on slides. If testing tells us it needs more time, the date moves. We don't trade durability for a date. It's the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology, together with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

Our work with Embraer is a CFM decision we took with Safran, and it rides on that same engine. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, the upgraded GEnx is in service for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: how the next few years play out across the industry. So we plan on the low case, we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole, and we're not starting anything new this year. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. No Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain, premium $0.

THE FRAME [CX-0467]. In 2030 the game was to get a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That is done. fps selected CFM (code 3, entry 2040). NGSA selected all three makers (code 7, entry 2037). The game now is the installed base on airframes already launched [CX-0422], and it is won on delivery, not on new launches. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564] holds until 2040.

THE GRID (brief §3). I checked it myself and Ghai confirmed every figure. Hold everything is -31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31 (S1 / S2 / S3): -46.08 on my weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20) and -56.00 on equal weights. It is the best plan in every column. Each alternative against hold (S1 / S2 / S3; my weights / equal):
- Ducted cancel: -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 (-16.04 / -16.54). It writes off $3.33B. Ghai's correction: it saves $2.67B on the board ($0.67B of R&D plus the $2B strain handed back) against about $18-20B of engine value given up.
- Embraer cancel: -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (-3.83 / -4.33).
- Open Fan: -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09 (-54.10 / -51.76). In S1 that is the $8B bill plus about $49.6B of wait penalty.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99 (-37.07 / -36.89).
- Lobby alone: about -1.00.
- Every combination with cancels is dominated.
Nothing on the menu is positive in any column, S1 included. Weights move the booking, not the decision.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: no order beats hold anywhere, so nothing is ordered.
- H3: the trigger is now on the record. GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and fitted on NGSA, so the Ducted stands as a defence by the book, and keeping it is worth +15.30 in the record column.
- H2: NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan. Every route waits in every column, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $35.99B against $15B, and even the allowance plus the full $4.0B game cap is $17-19B short.
- H5: RISE continues whole as technology. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel.
- Strain: no new project, so no new strain. Supply load is the live risk, but it is unpriced (see Ali).
- 20% and durability lines: unaffected. The Ducted is never called the next generation, and no durability margin is traded for the 2036 floor.
- Tie-break: not needed, since no alternative comes within ε.

LOW CASE FIRST [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, the selections on the record. I book low at the equal-weight -56.00 and treat S1's -31.20 as upside. Ghai agrees and would not go lower. We raise only when the next bulletin confirms the codes.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. Keeping the Ducted and Embraer continues decisions taken jointly in 2030. No reason exists why Safran would agree to a cancel: it would cut Safran's half of the same installed base. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. Any price, terms or narrowbody capacity commitment is joint [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, drove three parts. My record is silent on Embraer, so I followed doctrine (profile.md §6) and kept it, since a cancel runs against H1. My record has no lobbying evidence, so Lobby follows doctrine: only beside a live Open Fan. My record is silent on a Joint Venture and on Delay Tactics, so I followed profile.md §5 and §7: no public reaction and no price cut.

BIAS NAMED. My installed-base lens ('seed corn' [CX-0256], 'price of admission' [CX-0557]) pulls toward an Open Fan for the objective. Admission buys a seat, and here there is no seat to buy: both airframes are in service before 2045. My ramp optimism [CX-0590, CX-0592] is checked by publishing no Ducted rate and using the one year of board slack before 2038.

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND:
- A durability flag on the Ducted: the date moves; it is not cancelled.
- Supply that can't carry the Ducted's entry with LEAP on time: LEAP comes first, and the Ducted's ramp moves.
- A Joint Venture on the record: re-priced next round.
Investors asking does not move me [CX-0444].

No veto stands. Ghai's and Ali's vetoes all fall on orders I don't make, so there are no overrides.

memo_weighing.ops:

On supply and capacity his record is only my own description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked those parts against doctrine (dashboard_game.md §2 strain; LEAP OE and spares first).
On dates I deferred to him fully:

- An Open Fan could be ready no earlier than 2045, so it cannot make 2037 or 2040.

He raises no safety or durability flag on the Ducted, the LEAP fleet or RISE hardware, and gate calls stay cross-functional with Safran's engineers [CX-0012].
I adopted his slip arithmetic as his inference: a slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board, and a slip to 2038 costs about $1.2B PV, against $15-18B for a cancel. S1 (rivals hold), 0.60. The record carries the selections. Airbus's stated aim is CFM plus at least one other maker, and Boeing picked CFM. I expect P&W and RR to keep their solos on their published dates (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037).

S3 (fps to RR alone), 0.20. Boeing gave no signal of a switch, but a code is a request until entry, and RR would be ready by 2040. It costs $47.11B against S1. It is the worst column.

RISKS OUTSIDE THE COLUMNS (named, not booked):
(a) A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment. P&W says it has made none. RR said it would revisit in 2035 only if P&W's commitment were on the record. Both would need to commit in the same sealed round, so I put it at about 15-20% this round. On Ghai's reading it is worth +$7B to CFM if it folds in both solos on their dates, and -$14B if it stacks on top. On the stacked reading 'Dominate' fails even in S1 (about 46% in 2040).
(b) Rival ready dates slipping past NGSA's 2037 entry. That maker would be dropped and CFM would carry more of the slot. Upside I don't book.
(c) Our own Ducted slipping. A slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board; a slip to 2038 costs about $1.2B PV (Ali, inference). Embraer moves with it.
(d) Delay Tactics on the fps: Boeing -5 pp for 5 years from 2040, which cuts our fps slot in S1. It is covert, so we would see it only at game end. No reaction (doctrine).
(e) Raw materials: titanium forgings and rare earths for the Ducted's ramp. Unpriced and unquantified (Ali's flag).
(f) Codes lock after this round. The next bulletin tells us our column, and I raise the booking only then.

board_response.recommendation: R2-1 Safety and readiness: Ali to report the Ducted's 2036 gate and Embraer's 2037 date on test evidence, cross-functional with Safran's engineers; move the date rather than trade durability or cancel.
board_response.response:
Taken up in full.
- Ali confirms 2036 as launch + 6 and Embraer's 2037 as launch + 7, riding on the Ducted. Nothing is earlier.
- He raises no safety or durability flag on the Ducted, the LEAP fleet or RISE hardware.
- He also says plainly that his record holds no ducted turn-on, turn-off result. The test base is LEAP-1A HPT hardware (certified December 2024) and RISE (350+ tests, compact-core HPT blades in dust testing) [CX-0225, CX-0216, CX-0222]. So 2036 is a gate, not a promise, and the statement says 'not before 2036, reported against that gate on test'.
- Gate calls stay with one cross-functional team, with Safran's engineers [CX-0012, CX-0633]. Any flag reaches you before the next orders.
- A slip to 2037 costs nothing on the board and one to 2038 about $1.2B PV, against $15-18B for a cancel. If durability needs time, the date moves.

board_response.recommendation: R2-2 Keep what we launched: hold the Ducted and Embraer; show each cancel against hold in all three columns; a cancel would need a reason why Safran would agree.
board_response.response:
Taken up. Both are held, and the Ducted is the H3 defence now triggered on the record.
- Ducted cancel: -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 against hold (-16.04 on my weights, -16.54 equal). It writes off $3.33B. Ghai's correction: it saves $2.67B on the board, the strain included, against about $18-20B of engine value given up.
- Embraer cancel: -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (-3.83 / -4.33). It is 0.00 beside a Ducted cancel.
There is no reason on the record why Safran would agree to either, since both cut Safran's half of the same installed base. No cancel is ordered.

board_response.recommendation: R2-3 Keep RISE whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran; hold the Open Fan and Lobby; say plainly that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up; don't stretch the airframer-path test; RISE never cancelled for cost.
board_response.response: Taken up in full. open_fan and lobby_emissions are held. objective_note states that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up on the dashboard: 2035 is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050, and every route waits on the 2037 and 2040 entries. The cost would be $35.99B to $57.60B, above the $2.0B cap and the $15B RISE allowance, which stays unused. RISE continues whole as technology, 50-50 with Safran, with no program dividend and no date. It goes into product when an airframer wants it.

board_response.recommendation: R2-4 The customer comes first in the code revisit: on-time LEAP and spares, finish the supplier work, test-gated 2036 Ducted, private CFM offer on standard terms with Safran; nothing ordered only because a rival moved.
R2-5 Weights and risks: treat S1-S3 as plausible, give weights, book low (-56.00); name the Joint Venture risk and the 50% share line in S2 and S3.
board_response.response:
Taken up.
- Weights are S1 0.60 / S2 0.20 / S3 0.20, all three plausible. I book -56.00, the equal-weight figure, below my own -46.08.
- Joint Venture: named in predictions at about 15-20% this round. On Ghai's reading it is worth +$7B if it folds in both solos and -$14B if it stacks on top, which would take S1 to about 46% in 2040.
- Share line: about 36% in 2040 in S2, and about 20% in 2040 in S3 (17% in 2050, its worst year). No order restores it.

board_response.recommendation: R2-6 Keep the payout whole: no new R&D or strain; round-1 package about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room after at least 70% returned; premium $0 ($0 of $4.0B).
board_response.response: Confirmed by Ghai. This round has $0 of new R&D and $0 of new strain. The standing package is ($4B + $2B) / 6 = $1.00B a year over 2030-35, against $2.55B of room after returning at least 70% of about $8.5B of free cash flow, which leaves $1.55B of headroom. board_response.recommendation: R2-7 Public statement: no rival, no blame, no Open Fan or RISE date, no CFM price talk without Safran; 2036 as a test-gated floor; Ducted never the next generation; Embraer as a CFM decision with Safran; RISE when airframers and airlines want it.
board_response.response: Taken up. The statement names no rival and blames no one. It gives no Open Fan or RISE date and has no price or terms talk. It says the Ducted is 'not before 2036, reported against that gate on test' and that it 'isn't our next-generation engine'. It presents Embraer as 'a CFM decision we took with Safran'. It says RISE's entry 'is really not for us to say', since the airframers and their airlines decide. Ali and Ghai pass the dates and the terms.

board_response.recommendation: R1 (round-1 review): report the 2036 Ducted date every round as a test-gated floor, with turn-on, turn-off results and cross-functional gate calls with Safran's engineers; a flag comes before orders.
board_response.response: Answered this round. 2036 is reported as a floor at launch + 6, and no flag is raised. Ali is candid that his record holds no ducted core or hot-section result, so the floor rests on the LEAP-1A and RISE test base, and we say 'not before 2036', not 'on track'. board_response.recommendation: R1 (round-1 review): complete supplier readiness on the 9 suppliers and 15 sites before the Ducted load lands, so LEAP and spares are not crowded out.

board_response.recommendation: R1 (round-1 review): confirm the Ducted and Embraer through CFM's joint practice and present both as CFM decisions taken with Safran; any Embraer price or terms are joint.
board_response.response: Taken up. Holding both continues joint decisions, so there is nothing new to gate. Any Embraer or other CFM price or terms are joint [CX-0184].

board_response.recommendation: R1 (round-1 review): keep 2036 as a floor, never a promise; never call the Ducted the next generation; re-test the Ducted on the record and show rival launches and any Joint Venture; keep booking low.

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467, CX-0319] In 2030 the game was getting a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That part is done. Both airframes launched. fps selected us and enters service in 2040. NGSA selected all three engine makers and enters service in 2037. Our Ducted is due in 2036 and Embraer in 2037. The game now is the installed base on airframes that are already launched [CX-0422]. We play it on delivery, not on new launches. Each airframer can still change its code until its airframe enters service. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. Nothing on our menu wins a slot: hold is the best grid plan in every column (-31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31). We win by keeping what we launched and being on time with LEAP engines and spares. The 2036 Ducted has to be proven on test, not on slides, and every airframer gets a CFM engine on standard terms, priced together with Safran. "We don't have a birthright on that next order." [CX-0564] That still holds until 2040. We earn the order by delivering, not by spending. The one hard call is to say plainly that 'Introduce the Open Fan' is given up on the dashboard. We do that without touching RISE as technology. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD, 2035.
- fps (Boeing): launched 2030 on a 10-year ramp, entry 2040, code 3 (CFM alone).
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, entry 2037, code 7 (CFM, P&W and RR).
- P&W GTF2: launched solo, ready 2036. RR UltraFan NB: launched solo, ready 2037. Both are fitted on NGSA.
- Ours: Ducted ready 2036; Embraer partnership ready (counts) 2037; GEnx upgrade in service since 2033, counting from 2042 (no re-engine on the record).
- No Joint Venture commitment is on the record. P&W says it has made none. RR is 'open' and said it would revisit in 2035 only if P&W's commitment were on the record. It is not.
- Airbus revisits its NGSA code in 2035, judged on published ready dates, CFM's choice between Ducted and Open Fan, fps's code, and A320 engine delivery performance. Its stated aim is 'CFM and at least one other maker'.
- Observed shares from 2026 to 2034 were flat: NB engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0; WB engines GEnx 42 / Trent 58.

WHAT WE KNOW AND WHAT WE DON'T [CX-0436]. Last round I called S2: NGSA alone, on CFM plus P&W. The market gave us both airframes and three engines on NGSA. Our ΔPV moved from 0.00 to -31.20 (yield 80.5%). Of that, -25.20 is engine value, mostly NGSA's slot split three ways, and the rest is the round-1 R&D ($4B) and strain ($2B). That is the market, not our orders.

THE H3 TRIGGER IS NOW ON THE PUBLIC RECORD. Two rival new NB engines are launched and selected on NGSA. The Ducted is a defence by the book, and it earns in the record column: cancelling it costs $15.30B in S1.

OBJECTIVE. 'Dominate NB engines' (at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050) is met in S1, worst year 2040 at 55.9%. My reading of the public rules (inference; my arithmetic reproduces the brief's S1 path of 56.5 / 55.2 / 55.9) puts CFM at about 36% in 2040 in S2 and about 20% in S3. No order on this menu restores it. 'Introduce the Open Fan' (launched and ready by 2050) is not met. 2035 is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050, and every route waits on an airframe.

COLUMNS.
- S1: rivals hold. This is the record.
- S2: NGSA moves to code 2 (P&W alone), and Airbus's slot leaves CFM. It costs $27.30B against S1.
- S3: fps moves to code 1 (RR alone), and Boeing's slot leaves CFM from 2040. It costs $47.11B against S1.
In both S2 and S3 a rival selection takes our slot, and no lever we hold answers it. Read them hard: no birthright [CX-0564].

THE GRID. Hold everything is the best plan in all three columns. Every alternative loses in every column.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision).
It WOULD VETO:
- ducted: cancel (-15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 against hold; writes off $3.33B; no reason on the record why Safran would agree).
- partner_embraer: cancel (-3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44; vetoed together with a Ducted cancel).

- lobby_emissions: launch (falls with a vetoed Open Fan; does nothing alone).
- Any premium above $2.0B, and any RISE allowance used outside the airframer-path test.
It WOULD APPROVE hold on every field, which is not a Board item, plus unpriced customer moves: LEAP and spares on time, supplier readiness at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites, a private CFM offer on standard terms, and RISE continuing 50-50 as technology.
It EXPECTS:
- the expected column and weights;
- every alternative against hold, column by column;
- Ali's report on the 2036 and 2037 dates on test evidence, with any flag;
- Ghai showing $0 of new R&D and strain, and the run-rate against the room;
- the Safran gate;
- an objective_note that says 'Introduce' is given up;
- premium $0;
- the Joint Venture and rival-ready-date risks named;

GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, in service 2033 (2030 + 3). The grid counts it from 2042 because no re-engine is on the record, and never before 2035. Open Fan: held. tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted (advice)

tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2036. NGSA entry 2037: 1 year ahead. fps entry 2040: 4 years ahead. On the board the +10 pp counts from the year the engine is ready, once a new narrowbody is in service, so from 2037; the brief's 2036 row is still 76.0%. A one-year slip to 2037 therefore costs nothing on the board. A slip to 2038 loses the 2037 year: 10 pp x 4,000 is about 400 engines, about $3.04B nominal, or about $1.24B PV at 2026. Airbus weighs published ready dates, so any slip is reported early, in the next round.

ops.memo:
Real testing, not analysis. I report against last year's promise: Ducted not ready before 2036, launch plus six. That floor stands. Nothing earlier. It clears NGSA's 2037 by one year and fps's 2040 by four. The +10 pp counts only once a new narrowbody is in service, so a one-year slip costs nothing on the board; two years costs about 400 engines in 2037, roughly $1.2B. A cancel costs $15-18B. If durability needs time, the date moves. It is never traded.

What I can't show you: my record holds no ducted turn-on, turn-off result. What is in real testing is the base: LEAP-1A HPT hardware, turned on, turned off, certified; RISE, over 350 tests with an early durability focus; compact-core HPT blades in dust testing. So 2036 is a gate, not a promise. Say 'not before 2036', not 'on track'.

Embraer counts from 2037, launch plus seven, and rides on the Ducted. Slip the Ducted past 2037 and Embraer moves with it.

No safety or durability flag in the evidence. No single person can make a safety decision: gate calls stay cross-functional, with Safran's engineers.

Physics unchanged: a ducted engine gets less than half the gain. Not our next generation.
