decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year either. So let me tell you what we know and what we don't.

What we know: two new single-aisle airplanes are launched, and there is a CFM engine on both today. We don't take that for granted. We don't have a birthright on any order, so we earn it the way we always have, by delivering. That starts with the LEAP engines and the spares our customers need right now, on time. Spares don't crowd out new engines.

The new ducted engine that CFM and our partners at Safran launched five years ago stays on its gate: not before 2036. We report against that gate on test, not on slides. If testing tells us it needs more time, the date moves. We don't trade durability for a date. It's the right engine for the airplanes in front of us. It isn't our next-generation engine. That is still RISE. We're all in on that technology, together with Safran, and we're keeping it whole. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. The airframers and their airline customers will decide that.

Our work with Embraer is a CFM decision we took with Safran, and it rides on that same engine. Any airframer that wants a CFM engine can have one, and nobody gets locked out. On the widebody, the upgraded GEnx is in service for our 787 customers.

What we don't know: how the next few years play out across the industry. So we plan on the low case, we keep the balance sheet and our capital returns whole, and we're not starting anything new this year. You won't see us pointing fingers; you'll see us solving problems. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on every field. No Board item, $0 of new R&D, $0 of new strain, premium $0.

THE FRAME [CX-0467]. In 2030 the game was to get a new CFM engine in place before the next narrowbody. That is done. fps selected CFM (code 3, entry 2040). NGSA selected all three makers (code 7, entry 2037). The game now is the installed base on airframes already launched [CX-0422], and it is won on delivery, not on new launches. Both airframes enter service before the 2045 round, so this is the last round in which either code can move. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564] holds until 2040.

THE GRID (brief §3). I checked it myself and Ghai confirmed every figure. Hold everything is -31.20 / -58.50 / -78.31 (S1 / S2 / S3): -46.08 on my weights (0.60 / 0.20 / 0.20) and -56.00 on equal weights. It is the best plan in every column. Each alternative against hold (S1 / S2 / S3; my weights / equal):
- Ducted cancel: -15.30 / -16.67 / -17.65 (-16.04 / -16.54). It writes off $3.33B. Ghai's correction: it saves $2.67B on the board ($0.67B of R&D plus the $2B strain handed back) against about $18-20B of engine value given up.
- Embraer cancel: -3.09 / -4.45 / -5.44 (-3.83 / -4.33).
- Open Fan: -57.60 / -57.60 / -40.09 (-54.10 / -51.76). In S1 that is the $8B bill plus about $49.6B of wait penalty.
- Open Fan + Lobby: -37.34 / -37.35 / -35.99 (-37.07 / -36.89).
- Lobby alone: about -1.00.
- Every combination with cancels is dominated.
Nothing on the menu is positive in any column, S1 included. Weights move the booking, not the decision.

MY TESTS.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: no order beats hold anywhere, so nothing is ordered.
- H3: the trigger is now on the record. GTF2 and UltraFan NB are launched and fitted on NGSA, so the Ducted stands as a defence by the book, and keeping it is worth +15.30 in the record column.
- H2: NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan. Every route waits in every column, so there is no launch. The RISE allowance cannot cover it: the cheapest route costs $35.99B against $15B, and even the allowance plus the full $4.0B game cap is $17-19B short.
- H5: RISE continues whole as technology. Holding the Open Fan is not a RISE cancel.
- Strain: no new project, so no new strain. Supply load is the live risk, but it is unpriced (see Ali).
- 20% and durability lines: unaffected. The Ducted is never called the next generation, and no durability margin is traded for the 2036 floor.
- Tie-break: not needed, since no alternative comes within ε.

LOW CASE FIRST [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1, the selections on the record. I book low at the equal-weight -56.00 and treat S1's -31.20 as upside. Ghai agrees and would not go lower. We raise only when the next bulletin confirms the codes.

SAFRAN GATE (H7). Hold orders no CFM narrowbody move, so there is nothing to gate. Keeping the Ducted and Embraer continues decisions taken jointly in 2030. No reason exists why Safran would agree to a cancel: it would cut Safran's half of the same installed base. RISE continues as a 50-50 decision [CX-0166]. Any price, terms or narrowbody capacity commitment is joint [CX-0184]. GEnx is GE alone.

- Partner Embraer: counts from 2030 + 7 = 2037. It rides on the Ducted, which is ready in 2036.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not done. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% since 2026, and that is not where we want to be. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. We launched it in 2030, when we were named on a new single-aisle, and it is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. We will not compress the programme to make a date. If that date comes under risk, we will say so early, with the plan.

Control what you can control. The GTF fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers, ahead of GTF2. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection, and there are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. That commitment is ours alone. A Joint Venture forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits. That is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture would share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. The Joint Venture would carry GTF2's schedule, not reset it.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
THE DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr commit, premium_b 0, overrides empty.

1. Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073]
- GTF2 (launched 2030) is ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037 entry into service (code 7, which includes P&W). It would also be ready for fps's 2040 entry into service if Boeing moves to code 7 (S3).
- If the Joint Venture forms this round (S4), its engine is the folded GTF2. It is ready in 2036, not at formation + 6 = 2041, and UltraFan NB's 2037 does not pull it later.
- Eddy passes both of his veto grounds on rows A and B. The fold neither compresses nor resets GTF2, and its configuration stays frozen through certification.
- I name my own bias here. My operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024][PX-0098]. So I take Eddy's number, not mine: the one-year margin is not shown at risk on the board, and nothing proves it safe. His ground-1 veto binds the moment test data say otherwise.

2. Starting point: Eddy's proposal
Eddy proposes hold and commit. Mitchill recommends the same orders. No binding veto stands from either of them.

3. GTF2: HOLD. The cancel test, written out
- A cancel writes off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B in 2035 to save the last ~$0.33B. This is the last round a cancel exists, because GTF2 is ready in 2036 and the next round is 2045.
- Cancel row: -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -20.98 (S1) / +0.34 (S2) / -32.79 (S3) / -20.98 (S4). Weighted: -18.73.
- Break-even P(S2) is 0.98, or 0.83 beside a commit with all the remaining weight in S4.
- My lever rule cancels only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can, and an airframer that has named us is not harvested [PX-0064 read across, inference].
- The $0.34B gain in S2 is not worth hedging. A cancel would also turn credibility from met to not met.
- Not a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010].

4. Joint Venture: COMMIT
- The trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- Against hold the commit reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. That is never below Do Nothing, weighted +0.55, for $0 of new R&D, because GTF2's $2B folds into P&W's share.
- My record on a Joint Venture is Low and holds no evidence of my own. This is doctrine plus the grid, decided on Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback directs.
- I name my architecture loyalty bias ('the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]). It would keep me out. Here the Joint Venture does not replace the GTF; it carries it.
- For: 'the strength of this partnership is critical' [PX-0038], and partners carried 49% of the 2023 charge [P-1563]. IAE ended when the partners were not on the same new engine [P-1875]; here both are on NGSA.
- Rolls-Royce decides this round without seeing our order. The commitment therefore mainly puts P&W on the public record for Rolls-Royce's stated revisit. That is why S4 is weighted only 0.10.

5. Red-line flag (gear and core [P-1233]): REBUTTED, and its condition written into the terms
- The flag said 'joining RR's engine shares RR's, not yours'. That assumed we would join UltraFan. Here GTF2 folds in, so our technology is the one at stake.
- The order commits risk, investment and revenue sharing, not technology. The technology question sits in the terms, and the terms are on the record before Rolls-Royce can commit:
  - the gear and core stay one P&W module and one P&W team, with design authority through certification;
  - there is no technology licence.
- Counting the fold-in toward our $2B share transfers no intellectual property.
- Rolls-Royce rates its own geared IP [P-2004], so it has no claim on ours.
- Eddy confirms that module ownership works for a GTF2-based engine [P-1240]. If any design ever needs the gear or core handed over, his withdraw proposal stands, and we withdraw before formation.
- The flag is therefore rebutted on these terms. The terms are a public other move and part of the statement.

6. Mitchill's four grounds
- Ground 1 (dividend and debt): not engaged. The envelope passes, and the dividend and debt path are intact.
- Ground 2 (unselected engine): passes. GTF2 is selected.
- Ground 3 (terms): passes on the final text. Standard terms, no discounts, no subsidy of UltraFan, and the durability kit is sold.
- Ground 4 (unproven upside): passes. His round-1 objection named its own condition (a live Rolls-Royce code and a commit row never below hold), and both now hold. The booked number is -8.44. Nothing for S4 is booked, and no Joint Venture date beyond 2036 is given.
- His cancel objection rests on return, not on one of his grounds. I adopt it anyway, on my lever rule and the Board's would-veto list.

7. Tie-breaks
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on parts, ahead of GTF2.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] applies here on visible demand, a live selection. It is RTX-wide in my record; applying it to GTF2 is inference. It argues for holding, not cancelling.
- No rival's price entered the answer [PX-0055].

8. Shared source [P-0746]
NGSA's code 7 stays covered by the shared-source relief declared in round 1, as franchise defence, at 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292][PX-0058]. No order of ours changes a code this round.

9. Capital order
The dividend first, then debt to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. GTF2's last $0.33B is 5.5% of the ~$6B envelope [PX-0268], and the commit adds nothing. No stretch is used.

10. Premium: 0
- Hold/commit (B) is the best expected PV at -10.14, against -10.69 for hold/hold, -29.42 for cancel and -26.94 for cancel/commit.
- No doctrine-favoured order trails the best, and no objective premium is needed. The total is $0 against the $1B cap.

11. Disclosure
- The statement leaves out the round-1 promise to launch in any round we are named. It keeps 2036 and 'proven before entry into service' as standards we set, not claims.
- It offers GTF2 only where we can be ready by an airframer's entry into service. It says nothing on Airbus's code review or on any airframer's dates [PX-0062]. It puts the fleet and A320neo deliveries ahead of GTF2.
- Its only lever on S2 is product, time on wing and delivery performance. The board prices none of that.

12. Incrementalism
My incrementalism leans me to S1. It does not move the answer: B weakly dominates A on any weights, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98.

Keep `gtf2_solo: hold` through to the 2036 ready year, and write the cancel test into the rationale.
- Cancel row: -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -20.98 / +0.34 / -32.79 / -20.98.

This is the last round a cancel can be taken; after 2036 GTF2 is ready and the S2 risk can no longer be hedged, at a cost of only $0.34B in that column. This is the annual programme NPV review the Board kept in 2017, applied to GTF2. The Board does not cut a programme a customer has asked for.

Take the Joint Venture to the ExCo gate this round. Its public trigger is now met (NGSA code 7 includes Rolls-Royce), and `jv_with_rr: commit` is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51). It adds no R&D while GTF2 is live. It also puts P&W's commitment on the public record, which is Rolls-Royce's own stated condition for revisiting. Both partners now have a new narrowbody engine on the same airframe (GTF2 2036, UltraFan NB 2037), the alignment whose absence ended IAE. This is a recommendation; the decision is Eddy's proposal, Mitchill's gate and Calio's call.

Joint Venture terms. Share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms; partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge, and that is the model. P&W keeps the gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. Calio's rationale should address the red line, given that GTF2 folds in. Mitchill should test the terms on ground 3. If a Joint Venture design ever needs the gear or core handed over, Eddy's proposal to withdraw stands, and the Board would veto the commit.

Write a 2045 withdraw test into the plan. The commitment stands until withdrawn. By 2045, NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) will be in service, and the Board books no Rolls-Royce commitment it has not seen. If Rolls-Royce has not committed by then, test `jv_with_rr: withdraw` against hold on the 2045 grid. 'P&W and RR then hold equal NB shares' can cut either way once both engines are fitted.

Durability and readiness. Eddy should report GTF2's progress toward 2036 on test, not on slides: severe-environment testing, full life for life-limited parts, and time on wing. He should state plainly and at once if the one-year margin to NGSA's 2037 EIS is at risk. The fleet keeps first call on parts and shops. A Joint Venture must carry GTF2's schedule and must not compress or restart it.

Disclosure. Airbus revisits its NGSA code this round against published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance, so the statement matters, and it must not overclaim.
- Report GTF2 as in development and ready in 2036, six years from launch, with time on wing and full-life parts as standards to be proven before entry into service, not as proven claims.
- Offer GTF2 to any airframer on standard terms, with no discounts.
- Say nothing on Boeing's or Airbus's dates, rates or codes.
- If P&W commits, state it as P&W's own standing commitment, sharing risk and never the gear or core.
- Book no Rolls-Royce commitment, and give no Joint Venture engine date beyond GTF2's own 2036, so that Eddy's dating rule is respected.
This also takes up the round-1 recommendation to promise no more than the orders do.

Return, dividend and envelope.

frame.question:
Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Airbus has named us on NGSA (code 7, alongside Rolls-Royce and CFM). So GTF2 launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, one year before NGSA's planned 2037 entry into service. Two things make this round final. It is the last round in which either airframer can change its code before entry into service. It is also the last round in which GTF2 can be cancelled.

What we do not control: Airbus's code review (S2), Boeing's fps code (S3), and whether Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture (S4).

What we do control gives three questions for 2035:
1. gtf2_solo: do we hold the selected GTF2 through to its 2036 ready year, or cancel it, writing off $1.67B to save $0.33B?
2. jv_with_rr: the public trigger is now met, because a live code includes Rolls-Royce. Do we put a standing Joint Venture commitment on the record? The terms would share risk and investment, never the gear or core [P-1233], and GTF2 would fold in and keep its own schedule.
3. Disclosure: Airbus is reviewing its code against published ready dates and A320 engine delivery performance. What do we say, without claiming durability we have not yet proven on test?

Each order must pass the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035], then Neil's gate, then the Board.
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD, 2035 (bulletin)
- Airframes:
  - NGSA (Airbus) launched in 2030. EIS 2037, code 7 (RR, PW and CFM).
  - fps (Boeing) launched in 2030 on the 10-year path. EIS 2040, code 3 (CFM).
  - Both are live and not yet in service. Both enter service before 2045, so neither can change its code after this round.
- Engines:
  - P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready 2036.
  - RR UltraFan NB Solo: launched 2030, ready 2037.
  - CFM ducted: launched 2030, ready 2036.
  - CFM-Embraer partnership: ready 2037.
  - GEnx upgrade: in service since 2033.
  - Fitted if nothing changes: NGSA gets CFM + PW + RR; fps gets CFM.
- Rolls-Royce:
  - No jv_with_pw commitment on the record.
  - Its stance: 'open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms', 'not committing today', revisit in 2035 if P&W's commitment is on the public record.
  - Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so Rolls-Royce decides this round without seeing ours. A commitment from us would be public from the next bulletin.
- Airbus is revisiting its NGSA code this round. Its criteria:
  - published ready dates (GTF2, UltraFan NB or a Joint Venture engine) against the NGSA entry year;
  - CFM's choice between ducted and Open Fan;
  - Boeing's fps code;
  - A320 engine delivery performance.
- Observed NB engine share 2026-34: CFM 76% / P&W 24% / RR 0%, unchanged.

OUR POSITION (brief)
- ΔPV is -8.44 $B if nobody moves (-6.44 engine value, -2.00 GTF2 R&D). Yield 92.3%.
- On the hold row our NB share falls from 24.0% to 19.4% in 2037, when NGSA enters service with three engines. It then drifts to 16.8% by 2049.

OBJECTIVE STATUS
- Restore credibility: MET (GTF2 on NGSA).
- Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV >= 0): NOT MET at -8.44. No order of ours meets it. Only S3 (+3.37) does, and that is Boeing's choice.
- The Board's open round-1 recommendations: a narrower disclosure, a readiness report on test, and cash against the envelope.

Shane, you propose the engine orders. Please bring the following.

(1) Your proposal for gtf2_solo (hold or cancel) and jv_with_rr (hold or commit), with your reasoning.

(2) Readiness, on test rather than on slides (the Board's round-1 recommendation, still open):

(3) Joint Venture readiness with the fold-in. A folded GTF2 makes the Joint Venture engine ready in 2036, against formation + 6 = 2041. Confirm that:
- a fold neither compresses GTF2 nor resets its date;
- UltraFan NB (ready 2037) folding in does not pull the date.

(4) Architecture.

- Integrated products need integrated teams [P-1240]. Does a module split work for a GTF2-based engine?

(5) Pacing parts and capacity, with the fleet first. Weigh GTF2's production ramp for a 2037 EIS against GTF fleet support and A320neo deliveries; Airbus scores A320 engine delivery performance in its review. Cover powder metal, castings and MRO slots.

(6) Engineering load: GTF2 through to certification, the durability kit, and Joint Venture integration work with Rolls-Royce. Is that one programme or two?

(7) Your two veto checks (durability before EIS; parts and capacity), marked passed or failed for each row A-D. Also check my draft statement against your dating rule:
- no Joint Venture date beyond GTF2's 2036;
- no date earlier than 2036;
- durability stated as standards, not claims.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is Option B: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr commit, premium_b 0.

gtf2_solo: HOLD
- An airframer has named us. The Board does not cut a programme a customer has asked for, and neither do I.
- My lever rule is to cancel only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can.
- Cancel trails hold by $20.98B to $32.79B in three columns and gains $0.34B in one; it needs P(S2) of about 0.98.
- Writing off $1.67B to save $0.33B is not a responsible bet [PX-0010].
- Hold also keeps us eligible for fps if Boeing moves (S3, +3.37), the only column where Capitalise is met.

jv_with_rr: COMMIT, ON CONDITIONS
- My trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- The commit is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51) and adds no R&D. If the Joint Venture forms, its engine is the folded GTF2, ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS.
- I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture (Low). This is doctrine plus the grid, and I will decide on Neil's cash test and Shane's technical test.
- I name my bias: architecture loyalty ('the GTF is the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]) would keep me out. Here the Joint Venture does not replace the GTF; it carries it.
- For it: 'The strength of this partnership is critical' [PX-0038]; partners carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge [P-1563]; and IAE ended when the partners were not on the same new engine [P-1875]. Here both would be.

THE RED-LINE FLAG AND MY PROPOSED REBUTTAL
- The red line: 'You spread risk, you spread investment through JVs, but you don't share technologies' [P-1233].
- The commit is an order to share risk and investment. The technology question sits in the terms, and the terms are ours to set: the gear and core stay P&W's own module, with no technology licence.
- GTF2's fold-in counts our spend toward our $2B share. It does not transfer intellectual property.
- Rolls-Royce says it does not need partnership for capability and rates its own geared IP [P-2004], so it has no claim on ours.
- If Shane finds a design that needs our gear or core, his withdraw proposal stands and the commit goes. I keep the flag open until both memos confirm.

PREMIUM: 0
- The commit weakly dominates hold, so no doctrine premium is needed. Once the trigger is met, commit is the doctrine-favoured order on my lever rule.
- Objective: credibility stays met under hold. Capitalise is not met in any column we control; the commit narrows the gap in S4 (-2.93 against -8.44).

MY PROVISIONAL COLUMN READ (I will take Neil's weights)
- S1 0.62, S2 0.15, S3 0.08, S4 0.15.
- Expected PV: A -10.69; B -9.87; C -29.42; D -25.70.
- My incrementalism bias leans to S1. It does not move the answer: B is never below A, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98.

WHAT COULD CHANGE MY LEAN
- The commit comes off if:
  - Shane fails durability, or finds the fold compresses GTF2;
  - the terms need our gear or core;
  - Neil sustains a ground-3 or ground-4 veto. In that case I revise to A.
- Nothing on this grid moves me to a cancel.

PROPOSED OTHER MOVES
1. GTF durability kit for the installed fleet (public): sold on standard terms, with no dated AOG recovery [PX-0100][PX-0098][PX-0104].
2. Joint Venture terms (public, with the commit): share risk, investment and revenue; P&W's gear and core stay its own module; no technology licence; no subsidy of either partner's solo engine.
3. GTF2 readiness report to the Board each round (private): severe-environment testing, LLP life and time on wing, with a flag at once if 2036 is at risk.
4. Standing 2045 review (private): a withdraw test if Rolls-Royce has not committed.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public_statement)
'Let me start with what is not done. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. It launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. If that date comes under risk, you will hear it from us first, early, with the plan. Control what you can control. The GTF fleet keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection; we're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. It forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits; that is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture shares risk, investment and revenue. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence, and the Joint Venture carries GTF2's schedule; it does not reset it. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.'

If the commit is struck, the Joint Venture sentences become: 'We have made no Joint Venture commitment. Any partnership we enter would share risk and investment, never our gear or core.'

No weights change the commit: it is never below hold on any weights. On Calio's weights B is -9.87, on mine -10.14.

On hold against cancel, two things would move me:
- P(S2) of 0.98 or more on its own, or 0.83 beside a commit with all remaining weight in S4. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so nothing public can show this before we decide.
- Eddy reporting on test that GTF2 cannot be ready for NGSA's 2037 EIS. The rules then drop us, and the hold row reads like S2 in every column. That is his call. I would re-run the cancel on it, and at $0.34B the cancel saves little even then.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. If Airbus moves NGSA to code 5, we lose another $21.32B against rivals holding; no order of ours buys it back. My first read is that Airbus's review is about timing, a one-year margin. If it is about A320 delivery performance, it is more pervasive, and that is our record.

My weights: S1 0.67, S2 0.15, S3 0.08, S4 0.10. Expected PV: hold/hold -10.69; hold/commit -10.14; cancel -29.42; cancel plus commit -26.94.

Hold GTF2. The $1.67B is spent; the write-off is a charge, not cash. The only cash decision left is the last $0.33B in 2035, 5.5% of a $6B envelope. It protects a selected position worth $18.73B weighted over a cancel, which breaks even only at P(S2) of 0.98. This is the last cancel round.

Commit. The trigger is on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. Against hold the row reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. Its worst column is 0.00, and it adds $0 of R&D while GTF2 folds in. My round-1 ground-4 objection named its own condition. That condition is met, so the objection is cleared. I book nothing for S4: my booked number is -8.44 either way.

Conditions: standard terms, no subsidy of UltraFan, the gear and core stay ours, no Joint Venture date beyond 2036. Rolls-Royce decides without seeing us, so the real test is withdraw against hold on the 2045 grid.

Dividend covered, debt on its pre-ASR path, no stretch, premium 0.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo = hold; jv_with_rr = commit, on the technical conditions below. premium_b is not my field; I expect 0.

(1) WHY
- gtf2_solo hold.
  - Airbus has named us on NGSA (code 7). GTF2, launched in 2030, is ready in 2036, before NGSA's 2037 EIS. If Boeing moves to code 7 (S3), it is also ready before fps's 2040 EIS.
  - My lever rule: when a cancel is legal, my default is hold. I report whether GTF2 can still be ready by the EIS of a live airframe whose code includes P&W. It can: 2036 against 2037.
  - On the grid, cancel against hold reads -20.98 / +0.34 / -32.79 / -20.98. I flag the cancel test to Neil and Chris. I have no record on cancelling a programme, so the call is theirs.
  - Neither of my veto grounds applies to a cancel.
- jv_with_rr commit.
  - The trigger I set in round 1 is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
  - Both technical conditions pass. The Joint Venture engine is ready by NGSA's EIS (the folded GTF2, 2036, against 2037), and P&W keeps the gear and core.
  - Against hold the row reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51 (hold+commit -2.93 against hold -8.44 in S4), and it adds no new R&D.
  - This is doctrine plus the grid. I have no record of my own on a Joint Venture. The call is Calio's.

(2) READINESS, ON TEST
- I cannot give the Board the test report it asked for. The brief and bulletin hold no data on severe-environment testing, LLP life or time on wing, and the board models none. I will not fill that in.
- What the record shows: GTF2 is 'in development; ready 2036' (bulletin and brief §1), with no slip published.
- Margins: 1 year to NGSA's 2037 EIS; 4 years to fps's 2040 EIS if Boeing moves.
- Is the 1-year margin at risk? On the board, no. On the company's own prior, it is exposed:
  - The derivative slip prior is +1.5 to 2 years (profile.md §3), which would put GTF2 at about 2037.5-2038, past 2037.
  - My own Advantage date slipped about a year: mid-2024 planned, certified 2025.
  - I will not say 'no surprise coming'. That was my error in June 2023.
- Plainly: nothing in the brief shows 2036 at risk, and nothing in the brief proves it safe.
- My ground-1 veto binds the moment test data show GTF2 cannot reach full-life LLPs and its time-on-wing standard by 2037.

(3) JOINT VENTURE READINESS WITH THE FOLD-IN
- If it forms in 2035 (S4), formation + 6 = 2041. The folded GTF2 is ready in 2036 and the folded UltraFan NB in 2037. The rule takes the earliest, so the Joint Venture engine is ready in 2036.
- The fold carries GTF2's date. It does not reset it to 2041 or compress it below 2036. UltraFan NB's 2037 does not pull the date later.
- The engineering condition that makes this true in practice (inference): the Joint Venture engine for NGSA is GTF2's own configuration, frozen through certification. No Joint Venture design change enters GTF2's certification baseline before 2036. Any merged or UltraFan content comes later as a derivative, fully tested before its own EIS.
- If the Joint Venture forms in 2045 instead, GTF2 is already ready, so readiness is not at issue. The 2045 withdraw test is cash (Mitchill), not a ground of mine.

(4) ARCHITECTURE
- Yes, module ownership works for a GTF2-based engine, on one condition.
  - Integrated products need integrated teams, and the design team should mirror the product's architecture [P-1240].
  - The gear and core are the integrated system. They stay one P&W module, run by one P&W team, with design authority for the engine through certification and no technology licence.
  - Rolls-Royce shares risk, investment and revenue. Partners already carried 49% of the 2023 powder-metal charge [P-1563], and partner shops carry MRO capital (seat doctrine).
- The live risk is Rolls-Royce's own geared IP folding in beside ours [P-2004], and pressure to merge the two designs.
  - The rules allow a withdraw only before formation, so the terms must be on the record before Rolls-Royce commits. Calio's draft statement does this.
  - If a design ever needs our gear or core handed over, I propose withdraw while it is still open.
- Doctrine, not my record.

(5) PACING PARTS AND CAPACITY, FLEET FIRST
- Ground 2 passes. The brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem: NB engine share has held at 24.0% for 2026-34, 960 engines a year, with no inject.
- I have no 2035 count of pacing parts, AOG or castings and will not invent one. The board does not model parts.
- Advice, not a veto: the hold row steps from 960 P&W NB engines in 2036 to 775 in 2037. On the board, nearly all of those 775 are GTF2s from NGSA's EIS year. No factory makes that ramp in one year.
  - In practice the ramp runs on GTF2's commonality with the Advantage.
  - Powder metal: capacity built with records discipline. The 2015 ramp is where the contaminant came in [P-1040][PX-0039].
  - Castings: build up in steps, measured quarter by quarter [PX-0125].
  - MRO slots for the growing GTF installed base come first.
- Order of call:
  - the GTF fleet and A320neo deliveries first, ahead of GTF2 production hardware;
  - between those two, the daily choice on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0123][PX-0131].
- Airbus scores A320 engine delivery performance this round, so GTF2 does not take parts from A320neo deliveries.
- A shared three-way slot on NGSA is easier on pacing parts than a sole-source ramp (inference).

(6) ENGINEERING LOAD
- If the Joint Venture forms, it is one programme: GTF2 folds in.
- The durability kit has been in shop visits since 2026 and is mature.
- Joint Venture work with Rolls-Royce before 2036 is commercial, support and interface work. It does not change GTF2's certification baseline.
- Advice only: the board charges P&W no strain.

(7) VETO CHECKS BY ROW (ground 1, durability / ground 2, parts)
- A (hold / hold): pass / pass.
- B (hold / commit): pass (Joint Venture engine 2036 against 2037) / pass.
- C (cancel / hold): neither ground engaged, since no engine goes on an airframe; pass. I do not propose it.
- D (cancel / commit): pass / pass.
  - In S4 the Joint Venture engine would be the folded UltraFan NB, ready 2037 against EIS 2037. That is ready by EIS with zero margin, on an engine whose test programme I cannot see.
  - The Joint Venture engine would be Rolls-Royce's architecture, not an extended GTF.
  - Both are concerns, not binding.
- No binding veto.

STATEMENT CHECK (Calio's draft)
- It passes my dating rule:
  - 'launched in 2030 and is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch' gives no date before 2036;
  - it gives no Joint Venture engine date beyond 2036, and 'carries GTF2's schedule; it does not reset it' is right;
  - 'standards we have set ... still have to prove them on test' states standards, not claims.
- Advice, not binding:
  - Make the first-call line 'the GTF fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on our parts, shops and engineers, ahead of GTF2'. That matches Calio's own red line and Airbus's delivery criterion.
  - 'You will hear it from us first, early' is a promise I have to keep. My dated recoveries have slipped before.

decision.public_statement:
Let me start with what is not done. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has held at 24% since 2026, and that is not where we want to be. GTF2 is in development, not yet proven. We launched it in 2030, when we were named on a new single-aisle, and it is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch. Time on wing and full-life parts are the standards we have set for it, and we still have to prove them on test before entry into service. We will not compress the programme to make a date. If that date comes under risk, we will say so early, with the plan.

Control what you can control. The GTF fleet and A320neo engine deliveries keep first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers, ahead of GTF2. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

GTF2 is offered to any airframer where we can be ready by its entry into service, on standard terms. We will not buy a selection, and there are no launch-style discounts. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase.

Today Pratt & Whitney makes a standing commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on a new single-aisle engine. That commitment is ours alone. A Joint Venture forms only if Rolls-Royce also commits. That is Rolls-Royce's decision, and we book nothing until it does. Any Joint Venture would share risk, investment and revenue on aligned, standard terms. Pratt & Whitney keeps its gear and core as its own module, with no technology licence. The Joint Venture would carry GTF2's schedule, not reset it.

We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates, rates or engine choices. When we've seen it and when we feel good about it, we invest.
decision.rationale:
THE DECISION: gtf2_solo hold, jv_with_rr commit, premium_b 0, overrides empty.

1. Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073]
- GTF2 (launched 2030) is ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037 entry into service (code 7, which includes P&W). It would also be ready for fps's 2040 entry into service if Boeing moves to code 7 (S3).
- If the Joint Venture forms this round (S4), its engine is the folded GTF2. It is ready in 2036, not at formation + 6 = 2041, and UltraFan NB's 2037 does not pull it later.
- Eddy passes both of his veto grounds on rows A and B. The fold neither compresses nor resets GTF2, and its configuration stays frozen through certification.
- I name my own bias here. My operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0024][PX-0098]. So I take Eddy's number, not mine: the one-year margin is not shown at risk on the board, and nothing proves it safe. His ground-1 veto binds the moment test data say otherwise.

2. Starting point: Eddy's proposal
Eddy proposes hold and commit. Mitchill recommends the same orders. No binding veto stands from either of them.

3. GTF2: HOLD. The cancel test, written out
- A cancel writes off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B in 2035 to save the last ~$0.33B. This is the last round a cancel exists, because GTF2 is ready in 2036 and the next round is 2045.
- Cancel row: -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -20.98 (S1) / +0.34 (S2) / -32.79 (S3) / -20.98 (S4). Weighted: -18.73.
- Break-even P(S2) is 0.98, or 0.83 beside a commit with all the remaining weight in S4.
- My lever rule cancels only once no live airframe can still use GTF2 in time. NGSA can, and an airframer that has named us is not harvested [PX-0064 read across, inference].
- The $0.34B gain in S2 is not worth hedging. A cancel would also turn credibility from met to not met.
- Not a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010].

4. Joint Venture: COMMIT
- The trigger is met on the public record: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- Against hold the commit reads 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. That is never below Do Nothing, weighted +0.55, for $0 of new R&D, because GTF2's $2B folds into P&W's share.
- My record on a Joint Venture is Low and holds no evidence of my own. This is doctrine plus the grid, decided on Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback directs.

5. Red-line flag (gear and core [P-1233]): REBUTTED, and its condition written into the terms
- The flag said 'joining RR's engine shares RR's, not yours'. That assumed we would join UltraFan. Here GTF2 folds in, so our technology is the one at stake.

- The flag is therefore rebutted on these terms. The terms are a public other move and part of the statement.

6. Mitchill's four grounds
- Ground 1 (dividend and debt): not engaged. The envelope passes, and the dividend and debt path are intact.
- Ground 2 (unselected engine): passes. GTF2 is selected.

- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the fleet and A320neo deliveries keep first call on parts, ahead of GTF2.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] applies here on visible demand, a live selection. It is RTX-wide in my record; applying it to GTF2 is inference. It argues for holding, not cancelling.
- No rival's price entered the answer [PX-0055].

NGSA's code 7 stays covered by the shared-source relief declared in round 1, as franchise defence, at 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292][PX-0058]. No order of ours changes a code this round.

9. Capital order
The dividend first, then debt to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. GTF2's last $0.33B is 5.5% of the ~$6B envelope [PX-0268], and the commit adds nothing. No stretch is used.

10. Premium: 0
- Hold/commit (B) is the best expected PV at -10.14, against -10.69 for hold/hold, -29.42 for cancel and -26.94 for cancel/commit.
- No doctrine-favoured order trails the best, and no objective premium is needed. The total is $0 against the $1B cap.

11. Disclosure
- The statement leaves out the round-1 promise to launch in any round we are named. It keeps 2036 and 'proven before entry into service' as standards we set, not claims.
- It offers GTF2 only where we can be ready by an airframer's entry into service. It says nothing on Airbus's code review or on any airframer's dates [PX-0062]. It puts the fleet and A320neo deliveries ahead of GTF2.
- Its only lever on S2 is product, time on wing and delivery performance. The board prices none of that.

12. Incrementalism
My incrementalism leans me to S1. It does not move the answer: B weakly dominates A on any weights, and C needs P(S2) of about 0.98.

ops.note:
I CONCUR. Orders: gtf2_solo = hold; jv_with_rr = commit; premium_b = 0. These are the orders I proposed. No veto, no red-line breach.

FOR THE BOARD
- GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036 (bulletin and brief §1).
- Live airframes:
  - NGSA: EIS 2037, code 7, includes P&W. Margin 1 year.
  - fps: EIS 2040, code 3 (code 7 in S3). Margin 4 years.
- Joint Venture engine: if Rolls-Royce commits now (S4), it forms in 2035. The ready year is the earliest of 2041 (formation + 6), 2036 (folded GTF2) and 2037 (folded UltraFan NB), so 2036, against 2037. If it forms in 2045, GTF2 has been ready since 2036, so readiness is not at issue.
- Nothing I fail on durability or parts.

1. READINESS AND DURABILITY (GROUND 1): PASS
- hold keeps GTF2 on its six-year programme, ready 2036, before both EIS dates.
- commit carries GTF2's date into the Joint Venture without compressing or resetting it.
- The configuration freeze through certification is adopted as I asked: Joint Venture or UltraFan content comes only as a later derivative, tested before its own EIS.
- Test data: still none in the brief, so I give no figures. The 1-year margin is not shown at risk, and nothing proves it safe. On the company's 1.5-2 year slip prior it is exposed. That is advice, not binding.
- My ground-1 veto stands on any order or statement that dates GTF2 before 2036, dates the Joint Venture engine past 2036 while GTF2 is folded in, or presents a late engine as on time.

2. STATEMENT: PASS
- 'Due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch' gives no date before launch + 6.
- 'Standards we have set ... still have to prove them on test' states standards, not claims.
- 'We will not compress the programme to make a date' is right.
- 'Offered ... where we can be ready by its entry into service' fixes the round-1 overreach I flagged.
- It gives no Joint Venture date, and 'carry GTF2's schedule, not reset it' is correct.
- My first-call line is in: the GTF fleet and A320neo deliveries come ahead of GTF2.

3. PARTS AND CAPACITY (GROUND 2): PASS
- No live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem: P&W NB share is 24.0% for 2026-34, 960 engines a year, with no inject.
- No new launch this round. The board does not model parts.
- The private order of call is right: fleet MRO and A320neo deliveries first, powder metal with records discipline, castings in steps.
- The 960-to-775 step from 2036 to 2037 (mostly GTF2 on the board) stays a stepped plan, not a public promise.

4. CONTAIN FIRST: does not apply. The brief shows no quality escape.

5. ARCHITECTURE AND SINGLE AISLE: PASS. A GTF-based Joint Venture engine, no widebody.

ADVICE, NOT BINDING
- The public terms state a '$2B share' that comes from our private brief. Publishing it is Mitchill's call; it is not a ground of mine.
- 'We will say so early, with the plan' is a promise I have to keep. My dated recoveries have slipped before [PX-0115][PX-0128].

WHERE MY RECORD IS THIN
It is one event, June 2023, before the recall. The Joint Venture checks rest on the seat's doctrine, not on anything I've said myself.

Speaking for the seat: that's on us, and we've got this. We earn the dependable engine reputation every day.

other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney (the jv_with_pw: commit order). The terms: shared risk and investment, and each side's technology protected. Our UltraFan technology is protected the way P&W protects its gear and core. If P&W comes to the table, we form it; if not, UltraFan goes on alone. No ready date and no airframer date are given for any Joint Venture engine [RX-0118, RX-0072, R-1010].

other_moves.move: Joint Venture internal conditions (structure and maturity)
other_moves.detail: (1) RR funds nothing beyond its $4B share and carries none of P&W's costs. (2) If the Joint Venture forms, a folded programme keeps its own test clock and certification path. Internally the Joint Venture engine counts only at that programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036), and otherwise at formation + 6. (3) No new combined design is offered for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan and no core change. A gearbox change at year 5 of 7 would restart maturity testing. (4) Our support plan carries over unchanged, and we do not count on P&W's shops, because the GTF fleet keeps first call on them [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: 2045 withdrawal review of the standing commitment
other_moves.detail: If the Joint Venture has not formed by the 2045 round, we place a sealed jv_with_pw: withdraw in the 2045 orders, unless that round's grid shows the commit at or above hold. By then NGSA and fps are in service, so no live airframe could use a Joint Venture engine in time, and keeping it would be options management [RX-0051, R-1573]. No widebody item goes beside a standing commitment. The withdrawal goes in the same round as any Trent 1000 upgrade, so the $5B strain cannot come back.

other_moves.move: UltraFan NB test programme held to its seven-year clock
other_moves.detail: Launched 2030, ready 2037, which is year 5 of 7 now. Certification and maturity testing run 2035-37. Gearbox sizing was closed at design in 2030-32. Gearbox durability is the item the EIS-readiness review must clear. That review is in 2036 and stays private, with a final certification gate before the first engine is delivered. If a phase slips, the engine slips. At zero margin we accept not being fitted at entry rather than cut a test [RX-0296, RX-0284].

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support build: 2035 contracting (Watson's plan, step 4 due)
other_moves.detail: Placed in 2035: (a) partner-shop agreements on our Singapore joint-venture model near the launch operators, with no narrowbody MRO scale of our own [RX-0287]; (b) castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts with high-performing suppliers. Airbus is locking titanium forgings for its own ramp, so ours go now [RX-0286]. Repair technology continues alongside the test programme. The spares pool and field-service team stand up in 2036. The EIS-readiness review is in 2036. Support is in place before entry into service. The plan is resized if Airbus changes its code, and carries over unchanged if the Joint Venture forms. Capacity, as advice: 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes to our best suppliers, not spread thin.

other_moves.move: Round-1 plan for failure retired
other_moves.detail: NGSA still carries code 7, so the cancel trigger has not fired. Holding beats cancelling in every column, S2 included (-3.22). 2035 was the last round for a cancel before readiness. UltraFan NB is held to readiness [R-1573, R-1005].

other_moves.move: UltraFan demonstrator path and technology pull-through continue
other_moves.detail: UltraFan technology continues to feed the Trent fleet for time on wing. Public R&D money is used where available. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0094, RG-0065].

other_moves.move: Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
other_moves.detail: About £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline
other_moves.detail: No price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.

other_moves.move: Widebody franchise watch for 2045
other_moves.detail: RR widebody share is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, a headroom of 5.2 pp. The franchise test triggers in 2045 on any of three events: a rival-engined Re-engine on the record, a further CFM widebody gain, or a projection below 55%. The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, once UltraFan NB is out of development: against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium within $3B. UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap [R-1574, RX-0101].

rolls_royce.public_statement: So, let me be clear. UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development and on its seven-year clock: ready in 2037, seven years from launch, and not before. The full test programme runs and nothing is compressed. If a phase slips, the engine slips. Support goes in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership has always been our preference, and today we put it on the record: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms. That means shared risk and investment, with each side's technology protected. We are actually bringing a technology. If Pratt & Whitney comes to the table, we form it. If not, we deliver on our own. Widebody is our franchise. There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
rolls_royce.rationale:
So, the decision, by the team rule.

1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL. ultrafan_nb_solo: hold, which keeps the programme to readiness with no cancel. jv_with_pw: commit. ultrafan_wb: hold. t1000_upgrade: hold. Both memos recommend exactly these orders, and the Board says it would approve them.

2. BINDING VETO CHECKS.
- CFO. McCabe co-signs the commit against the hurdle. It is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 against 'UltraFan NB: hold', +0.23 expected, worst column 0, with no new cash in any column. She withholds her signature on the upgrade, on UltraFan WB and on a commit beside either widebody item. None of these is ordered. She invokes no balance-sheet veto. The remaining $2.29B of Solo spend ($8B x 2/7, about $1.14B or £0.84bn a year in 2036-37, £1.68bn in total) comes from free cash flow, after the 2026-28 returns programme and inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. No equity, no borrowing, leverage at or below about 1.5x.
- Civil. Watson invokes no Civil veto. UltraFan NB, ready 2037 (2030 + 7), against NGSA's 2037 EIS is zero margin: a pass with a note. His concurrence rests on three conditions, and all three are met in these orders.
  (a) The public statement gives no UltraFan NB date before 2037, no Joint Venture ready date and no airframer date. 2037 is not placed next to NGSA, and the date is framed as a clock, 'not before'.
  (b) I count the Joint Venture engine only at a folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, or GTF2 2036) and otherwise at formation + 6 (2041). I promise no new combined design for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan, no core change. The folded programme keeps its own test clock (private other move).
  (c) The support plan is carried as a private other move with its dates. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox contracts are placed in 2035. The spares pool and field service stand up in 2036, and the EIS-readiness review is in 2036.
- No binding veto stands, and overrides is empty.

3. GRID, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5). My weights, which McCabe confirmed: S1 0.55, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05.
- S2 is a signal: Airbus's 2035 code review is on the record.
- S3 and S4 have nothing on the record.
- S5 sits below 'nothing': Boeing has said no second development, and Airbus says the A350 family is its focus.
Item by item:
- JV commit ('hold + commit to JV' minus 'hold'): 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights and on the Board's case (0.55 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.10); +0.11 to +0.46 with S4 at 0.05-0.20. Worst column 0, against a $4B limit. In S4 the whole +2.29 is spend not made: the $1.71B beyond our $4B share is already spent, sunk, with no new cash.
- Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.02 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.02 (-6.03 beside the JV) / -5.87. Expected -6.01, worst -6.03. That is beyond its own $2B bill and above the $3B cap, and it is a red line. Not ordered.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -6.95. Expected -8.90, worst -9.00. There is no Re-engine on the record, it overlaps UltraFan NB, and it is far above the $1B sub-cap. Not ordered.
- Cancel UltraFan NB: -24.54 / -3.22 / -42.25 / -24.54 / -24.54. Expected -22.05 (-19.99 beside the JV, -4.00 in S4). Worst -42.25. NGSA's code 7 flies it. Not ordered.
Row EVs: 'hold + commit to JV' +15.99; hold +15.76; 'hold + JV + T1000' +9.98; 'hold + T1000' +9.75; 'hold + JV + UltraFan WB' +7.09; 'hold + UltraFan WB' +6.87; 'cancel + JV' -4.00; cancel -6.28.

4. EXPECTED SCENARIO AND BEST PLAN. I expect S1, rivals hold. Its best plan is 'UltraFan NB: hold' at +18.26, tied with 'hold + commit to JV' at +18.26. The commit is best or tied-best in every column and best outright in S4 (+20.55). Premium $0B.

5. OFF-GRID (inference, nothing booked). If S3 and S4 come in the same round, equal shares could hand P&W up to about $8.9B of the fps upside, at a joint weight of about 0.01. If S2 and S4 come together, the Joint Venture keeps us on NGSA and recovers about $10.7B, at a joint weight of about 0.02. Net about +0.12. The two roughly offset, the S2 hedge is the larger, and the sign of +0.23 does not change. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so P&W cannot time its commit to Boeing's or Airbus's code.

6. WHY COMMIT, ON MY RECORD. 'We don't commit that easily' [RX-0124], so I do not take this lightly. The commitment costs nothing in any column, and an airframe can use it: NGSA's live code 7 includes both makers, and a 2035 formation is ready by 2037 from the folded UltraFan. So it is a choice, not options management [RX-0051]. Partnership is the preference, not a need [RX-0118]. The terms credit what we bring [RX-0072]: shared risk and investment, our technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core. It saves the last $2.29B if P&W comes in, which is cash as an input [RX-0042]. The test is binary [RX-0050]: P&W comes to the table, or we deliver alone. It is not open-ended. A sealed withdrawal is planned for 2045 unless that grid shows the commit at or above hold, and no widebody item goes beside it. The thresholds and the Joint Venture terms are doctrine and inference, not my record: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms.

7. RED LINES, CHECKED AGAINST THE FINAL ORDERS.
- No cancel of a flown programme: met.
- No widebody item beside UltraFan NB in development: met. Strain $0.
- jv_with_pw commit: met on the partner test (NGSA's live code 7 includes P&W), co-signed, with no Civil veto and no widebody item beside it.
- No early date and no airframer date: met.
- No item loses more than its own bill: the commit's worst column is 0.
- Premium within cap: $0B.
- No price concessions.
No colleague flagged a red-line breach against these orders. The flags both raised (upgrade, UltraFan WB, cancel) apply to options that are not ordered.

8. CAPACITY AND THE FRANCHISE (advice). Narrowbody volume is 965 engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes through partner shops and our best suppliers. Widebody is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, so the franchise holds above 50%. The franchise test comes back in 2045.

Remaining Solo spend is about £0.84bn a year, £1.68bn in total, funded from free cash flow with no balance-sheet veto. Her withheld signatures on the upgrade, UltraFan WB and any commit beside a widebody item are binding, and I respect them: none is ordered. I adopt both of her conditions as private other moves: a sealed withdraw in 2045 unless that grid shows the commit at or above hold, and nothing widebody beside a standing commitment. I also adopt her off-grid bound (S3+S4 -0.09 against S2+S4 +0.21) and book nothing from it. On cash, the hurdle and the downside, her test is my evidence.

I take his advice to place forgings contracts now, given Airbus's lock on titanium, and not to count on P&W's shops. I also take his 2045 sequencing: withdraw in the same round as any upgrade, so the strain does not return. His capacity view is advice and is carried in the support move.

recommendations.text: Keep UltraFan NB to readiness. Describe it publicly as ready in 2037, seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed. Make no price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps: narrowbody is an option, not a need, and we are not after share.

Watson's 2035 memo should report on the support plan he undertook in 2030. That covers the partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model; castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers; gearbox sizing, the one item that would turn the zero margin into a maturity concern; confirmation that no test phase has been cut to hold 2037; and the date of the EIS-readiness review. Capacity is advice, not a ground: the brief shows 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 against our 197 widebody a year.

McCabe should give weights for S1-S5 and the worst column for each item. She should give the remaining Solo spend (about $2.29B, roughly $1.14B a year to 2037). If a Joint Venture is ordered, she should give the cash and write-off effect of a 2035 formation, in which the live Solo folds in and spend beyond our $4B share is written off. She should confirm the fit with a broadly flat R&D envelope, the 2026-2028 returns programme and leverage at or below about 1.5x.

On the Joint Venture: we would approve a commit, but we do not press it; the CEO has said he dislikes options management. If he brings it, the terms should be aligned: shared risk and investment, our UltraFan technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core. The rationale should also address a case the grid does not show: Boeing naming RR (S3) and P&W committing (S4) in the same round. Under a formed Joint Venture, RR and P&W hold equal narrowbody shares, so part of the S3 upside would be given up. Finally, set a withdrawal review for 2045. If the Joint Venture has not formed by then, NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) will be in service and no live airframe can use its engine in time. A later formation would also bring the $5B strain back onto any widebody item.

Hold both widebody items this round. Revisit the Trent 1000 upgrade in 2045, when UltraFan NB is ready and no longer in development: either against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium inside $3B. UltraFan WB waits for a Re-engine on the record and must come within the $1B sub-cap. Without strain it is still -1.95 against a Re-engine and -4.00 without one. Watch the GEnx upgrade (55.2% from 2042) and any rival-engined Re-engine, which would trigger the franchise test.

Public statement: UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development, ready in 2037, with nothing compressed and support through partner shops before entry into service. Put no date beside any airframe. If committing to the Joint Venture, describe it as aligned terms with no ready date. 'We do not want to underestimate the risks.'

Other moves: keep the UltraFan demonstrator path and Trent fleet durability as public, qualitative moves. Retire the round-1 plan for failure: NGSA still carries our code, holding beats cancelling in every column (S2 included), and 2035 is the last round in which a cancel is possible before UltraFan NB is ready.

frame.question: So, the 2035 question, put in cash and quality of earnings. We have $5.71B in an UltraFan NB that NGSA's code 7 flies. It is ready in 2037 against NGSA's 2037 EIS, which is zero margin. On hold the board gives us +18.26 and both legs of the objective. The question is narrow. Do we protect what is working and add nothing? Or do we add one item: a Joint Venture commitment that costs nothing in any column and avoids the last $2.29B of Solo spend if Pratt & Whitney comes in? Everything else on the grid destroys value or breaks a red line. The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.02 and UltraFan WB is -9.00, because the $5B strain beside a narrowbody programme takes each beyond its own bill. A cancel is -24.54 in S1 and -42.25 in S3 on a programme an airframe flies. We are not after market share [RX-0054, R-1582]. We won't do anything not profitable [RX-0058].

Proposal: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` (kept to readiness, no cancel); `jv_with_pw: commit`, on aligned terms; `ultrafan_wb: hold`; `t1000_upgrade: hold`.

So, frankly, this round is about delivery, not new bets. UltraFan NB stays on its seven-year clock with the full test programme; NGSA flies it, and cancelling it would be value destruction in every column.

The Joint Venture is the one addition.
- It is never below hold: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights, worst column 0, premium $0B.
- It avoids the last $2.29B of Solo spend if Pratt comes in, which is cash as an input [RX-0042].
- NGSA's code 7 flies both makers, so a live airframe can use it: a choice, not options management [RX-0051].

- The terms must credit what we bring: shared risk and investment, our UltraFan technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core.
- A withdrawal review is set for 2045: if it has not formed by then, no live airframe can use it, and it goes.

- Helen withholds her co-signature, or her off-grid reading puts the S3+S4 giveaway above the S2+S4 hedge; or

Widebody: nothing this round. The upgrade comes back in 2045, once UltraFan NB is ready.

Other moves:
- Public: the UltraFan demonstrator path and Trent fleet durability continue.
- Private: Rob's support build and contracting status; pricing discipline (no concessions to keep NGSA or win fps); the round-1 plan for failure retired.

Draft public statement: 'So, UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development and ready in 2037, seven years from launch, with the full test programme and nothing compressed, and support in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership has always been our preference, and today we put it on the record: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, sharing risk and investment, with each side's technology protected. If Pratt & Whitney comes to the table, we form it. If not, we deliver on our own. Widebody is our franchise: no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.'

If we hold the JV instead: 'Partnership remains our preference; we are open to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms, and we are not committing today.'

Subject to Helen's co-signature and Rob's ready check.

No new cash in any column. ultrafan_nb_solo hold: the hold row's worst column is S2 at -3.06 against the status quo, inside the $8B bill, and holding still beats cancelling there by 3.22. tests.name: Capex a year in £ (CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: Informational: my evidence sets no threshold.

That is about $1.14B a year, about £0.84bn a year at 1.36 $/£, and about £1.68bn in total, equal to 22-23% a year of FY2026 FCF guidance of £3.6-3.8bn. tests.numbers: Recommended orders: the $2.29B is the tail of a programme inside the envelope since 2030, so it is redeployment, not new money. The commit adds nothing and saves $2.29B in S4. Leverage stays at or below about 1.5x. Board parameters: debt $40B on EV $110B. No order needs funding beyond cash, so no balance-sheet veto is invoked.

tests.name: Joint Venture cost against Solo (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: A commit after a Solo is live folds the Solo in: spend beyond RR's $4B is written off and RR's and P&W's narrowbody shares are equalised. The grid row includes both: read it against hold and do not deduct them again.
tests.numbers: Formed in 2035: $5.71B is spent and our share is $4B. The $1.71B beyond our share is written off, but it is already spent: a sunk cost, no new cash. The remaining $2.29B is not spent. Total R&D falls from $8.00B to $5.71B. The grid's +2.29 in S4 equals $8B x 2/7 exactly. So on this board the whole S4 gain is avoided spend, and equalising shares leaves RR's engine value unchanged in S4. Confirmed. Against Solo: the Joint Venture needs no further cash, where Solo still needs $2.29B. It is ready in 2037 from the folded UltraFan, or 2036 if GTF2 folds in (Watson to confirm).

tests.name: Off-grid joint cases: S3+S4 and S2+S4 (CEO ask 5, inference)
tests.threshold: Advice. The grid does not price joint columns. Bound them from the grid swings and book nothing.

S3+S4: RR's S3 uplift over S1 is +17.71 (35.97 - 18.26), so equal shares could hand P&W up to about half of it, about $8.9B. S2+S4: RR's S2 drop is -21.32 (18.26 to -3.06), so equal shares could recover at least about half, about $10.7B. Taking the columns as independent, the joint weights are about 0.01 (0.10 x 0.10) and 0.02 (0.20 x 0.10). That gives about -0.09 against about +0.21, a net of about +0.12. The two roughly offset, the S2 hedge is the larger, and neither changes the sign of +0.23. Moves are sealed and simultaneous, and Airbus's 2035 code choice cannot see our 2035 commitment. Answer: the standing commitment earns its +0.23 once both are counted. I book none of it.

tests.threshold: State when each order starts to earn. The brief gives no payback years (inference).

A Trent 1000 upgrade launched in 2035 earns not before 2042 without a Re-engine. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2041 but earns only with a Re-engine in service.

Next rows: 'hold + JV + T1000' +9.98, 'hold + T1000' +9.75, 'hold + JV + UltraFan WB' +7.09, 'hold + UltraFan WB' +6.87, 'cancel + JV' -4.00, cancel -6.29. vetoes.ground: Advice, not a sign-off ground, because a cancel is neither a launch nor a commit. I would not support it.
