cfo.would_change_mind_if: I would move the Joint Venture commit to hold, as option B with the $0.23B premium declared, in these cases. Watson invokes a Civil veto: a fold compresses a test phase, gearbox sizing is not closed, or support is not in place before 2037. The commit is ordered beside a widebody item. The terms the CEO proposes would have RR fund beyond its $4B share or carry P&W's costs. I would also change my view if the CEO set S3 (Boeing naming RR on fps) well above S2. The off-grid S3+S4 give-up (up to about $8.9B at about 0.01 joint weight) would then outweigh the S2+S4 hedge (about $10.7B at about 0.02), and the standing commitment would have to earn its place on more than +0.23. In 2045 I withdraw the commitment unless that round's grid shows it at or above hold: once UltraFan is ready there is no spend left to avoid. I would reopen the widebody items in the 2045 round, with UltraFan NB ready and no Joint Venture standing. That means the Trent 1000 upgrade against a Re-engine on the record or a declared premium within $3B, and UltraFan WB only against an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine with UltraFan named, within the $1B sub-cap. Nothing would make me support a cancel of a programme a live airframe flies.
cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then we said the balance sheet. This round is about delivery: protect what is working.

Weights: I confirm S1 0.55, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05. I keep 0.20 on S2: it is our plan-for-failure column.

UltraFan NB stays at hold. About $2.29B remains: roughly $1.14B a year to readiness, about £0.84bn or 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance, £1.68bn in total. It is the tail of a programme already inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, funded from cash: no equity, no borrowing. Holding beats cancelling in every column, by 3.22 even in S2. A cancel writes off $5.71B and is -22.05 expected. I would not support it.

I co-sign the Joint Venture commit. Against hold it is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0: +0.23 expected, worst column 0, no new cash in any column. The +2.29 is exactly the spend we would not make; the $1.71B beyond our share is already spent. My conditions: a sealed withdrawal in 2045 unless that grid shows it at or above hold, and nothing widebody beside it.

I withhold my signature on the Trent 1000 upgrade (-6.01 expected, worst -6.03) and UltraFan WB (-8.90, worst -9.00). Both lose more than their own bill.

My record is thin on engine-launch economics: these are the board's numbers. So hold it this way: $2.29B out, nothing booked for the Joint Venture, any saving upside. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: UltraFan NB Solo (live, held to readiness), with the 2035 status report
tests.threshold: Ready year = launch + 7, and it must be no later than the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin passes with a note; it is not a fail and not a veto ground. A later ready year fails, and that fail is advice only.
tests.numbers: Launched 2030, ready 2037 (2030 + 7). NGSA: launched 2030, code 7, EIS 2037, so the margin is 0 years. Pass, with a note. fps: launched 2030 on the 10-year path, EIS 2040, code 3 (CFM). RR is not selected on fps; if Boeing named RR (S3) there would be 3 years in hand. STATUS REPORT 2035 (end of year 5 of 7). Pacing as adopted in 2030: years 1-2 (2030-32) detailed design and gearbox sizing; years 3-5 (2032-35) ground and flight test; years 6-7 (2035-37) certification and maturity testing. No phase has been cut: the bulletin's ready year is exactly launch + 7. Gearbox sizing: closed at design under that pacing (inference: the board does not model it). What is still to be proven is gearbox durability in maturity testing, and the EIS-readiness review must clear it. EIS-readiness review: 2036, a year before EIS, kept private, with a final certification gate before the first engine is delivered in 2037. If a phase slips, the engine slips. At zero margin, a slip means RR is not fitted at NGSA's entry, and we accept that rather than cut tests. S2 check (CEO's ask): the hold row is -3.06 against R&D of -8.00, so the board still credits about +4.94 of engine value. That value is all narrowbody, because S2 leaves widebody unchanged. RR's narrowbody share therefore stays above 0 in 2045 and 2050, at far lower value. That is inference from the grid; the brief gives no S2 shares by year. I confirm the arithmetic, not an airframe seat, and the support build would be resized to match.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: Joint Venture with P&W (`jv_with_pw: commit`)
tests.threshold: Ready at formation + 6. It can be earlier only if a partner folds in a programme that is further along, at the date the bulletin shows. It must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves.
tests.numbers: P&W has not committed. In S1, S2, S3 and S5 nothing forms and the commit is 0 against hold. If formed in 2035 (S4), formation + 6 is 2041 on its own, which is too late for NGSA (2037) and fps (2040). The folded programmes are further along: UltraFan NB is ready 2037 and GTF2 2036 (bulletin). So the Joint Venture engine is ready in 2036-37, by NGSA's 2037 EIS with 0-1 years of margin. That is consistent with the grid's +2.29 in S4. CONDITION: the folded programme keeps its own test clock and certification path. A new combined design is formation + 6 = 2041 and must not be offered for 2037; examples are UltraFan with P&W's gear, or core changes. P&W's gearbox is not on offer ('never our gear or core'). A gearbox change at year 5 of 7 would restart gearbox maturity testing, so the Joint Venture does not ease our sizing risk for 2037; the gearbox closes inside our own programme. Formed in 2045 instead, it would be ready in 2051, after NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are in service. No live airframe could use it, which is why the 2045 withdrawal is needed. The fold's write-off ($1.71B beyond our $4B share) and the $2.29B not spent are McCabe's to price.

tests.name: Ready by EIS: widebody items (UltraFan WB, Trent 1000 upgrade)
tests.threshold: UltraFan WB is ready at launch + 6 and counts only once a re-engined 787 or A350 is in service. The upgrade counts at launch + 3, and not before the first Re-engine's EIS (2042 if neither re-engines).
tests.numbers: Both held. UltraFan WB launched in 2035 would be ready in 2041, but there is no Re-engine on the record, so it would count for nothing. The upgrade launched in 2035 would count from 2042 (launch + 3 is 2038, but no Re-engine is on the record), for +5 pp of widebody. Launched in 2045 instead, it counts from 2048 with no strain if no narrowbody project is live.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB, or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the earlier date the bulletin shows for a folded programme). Nothing on any airframer's dates.
tests.numbers: Draft statement: 'ready in 2037, seven years from launch'. That is 2030 + 7, so not early. It gives no Joint Venture ready date and no airframer date, and puts no 2037 next to NGSA. The fallback statement ('open to Pratt & Whitney ... not committing today') also passes. Advice (a note, not a veto): treat 2037 as a clock, not a target ('not before'), so the date never becomes a reason to cut a test. The rationale may state the Joint Venture's ready year privately, as the folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037 or GTF2 2036) or otherwise 2041. Never put a 2036 date on an RR engine in public. The 2036 EIS-readiness review date stays private.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale (a briefing constraint), so a support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (inference).
tests.numbers: Status of the plan adopted in 2030 (the board does not model support, so this is inference). Step 4 falls due this round: partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model near NGSA's launch operators, and castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts with high-performing suppliers (GBP 685M of GBP 2.5bn spend in 2023). Both are placed in 2035. Step 2: repair technology continues alongside the test programme. Step 3: the spares pool and field-service team stand up in 2036. Step 5: EIS-readiness review in 2036. Support is in place before 2037 if the CEO carries these as a private other move with their dates; his initial lean lists 'Rob's support build and contracting status', and the draft statement says 'support in place through partner shops before entry into service'. Airbus's public move to lock titanium forgings and rare earths for its own NGSA ramp means our forgings contracts go now, not in 2036 (inference). If the Joint Venture forms, the support plan carries over unchanged. Do not count on P&W's shops: the GTF fleet 'keeps first call on our parts, our shops and our engineers' (P&W statement). If the plan is dropped from the final orders, ground (c) applies and binds.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project (UltraFan NB or Joint Venture) beside a widebody project (UltraFan WB or upgrade) costs $5B of strain; flag the years of overlap. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (seat and company rule, inference).
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB is in development 2030-37. Plan A (hold + JV commit) has no widebody item: strain $0 and 0 years of overlap. If the Joint Venture forms, the Solo folds into it, so there is no second narrowbody project and no added strain. C, the upgrade launched 2035 (2035-38), overlaps UltraFan NB for 2 years (2035-37). Against hold it is -6.02 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.02 / -5.87 (-6.03 in S4 beside the JV), below its own -$2B bill in every column, and it breaks a red line. D, UltraFan WB launched 2035 (2035-41), also overlaps for 2 years. It is -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -6.95, with no Re-engine on the record, and it breaks a red line. Confirmed: nothing widebody until UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, so the upgrade waits for the 2045 round. Caution: a standing commitment that forms in 2045 would start a narrowbody project (formation + 6 = 2051) beside a 2045 upgrade and bring back the $5B strain. So the withdrawal belongs in the 2045 orders, the same round as any upgrade (inference; the rules do not say whether an UltraFan that is already ready still folds).

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so this is not applicable unless the brief reports a constraint. Flag partner MRO and high-performing supplier needs as advice.
tests.numbers: Brief, on hold. Narrowbody: 965 engines in 2037, 978 in 2038, a 990 peak in 2039, 863 a year from 2049. Widebody: 197 a year to 2041, 188 from 2042. RR total: 1,162 in 2037 and 1,187 in 2039. Narrowbody alone is 4.9 times widebody (5.0 at the peak). My midterm OE ramp was 300-350 a year; 2024 actuals were 529 OE, of which 278 were widebody. On the board, output steps from 197 to about 1,162 in a single year, and no constraint is reported. Advice: concentrate castings, forgings and gearbox work with high-performing suppliers, and build MRO through partner shops, not capacity spread thin. Shop visits: I use my 1,100-1,200 a year, not Helen's 1,400-1,500 (never reconciled). In S4 (equal shares with P&W), RR's volume changes and the ramp plan is resized.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers: 2040: 58.0%. 2045: 55.2%. 2050: 55.2%. The worst year is 55.2% from 2042, after the GEnx upgrade counts, which leaves 5.2 pp of headroom. In S5 the hold row is +18.17 against +18.26 (-0.09). I read that as the GEnx upgrade counting from the Re-engines' 2040 EIS instead of 2042 (inference), which is still above 50%. Nothing forces widebody spend now: no Re-engine is on the record and Airbus says the A350 family is its focus. The franchise test triggers in 2045 on any of: a rival-engined Re-engine on the record; a further CFM widebody gain (5.2 pp is about one more CFM move); or a projection below 55%. Then the upgrade comes first, once UltraFan NB is out of development. Trent fleet durability continues as funded.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An idle or cancelled UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively only; grid values are never adjusted for it.
tests.numbers: Qualitative. The UltraFan demonstrator path and Trent fleet durability (about GBP 1bn over four years) continue as public other moves, and some UltraFan technology feeds today's Trent fleet for time on wing. This is no argument for a cancel: the live programme already feeds the fleet. No grid value is changed.

vetoes.plan: A: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` + `jv_with_pw: commit`, with `ultrafan_wb` and `t1000_upgrade` at hold
vetoes.ground: No Civil veto invoked. UltraFan NB's 2037 ready year against NGSA's 2037 EIS is zero margin: a pass with a note, not a veto. A Joint Venture formed this round takes a folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037 or GTF2 2036), so it is ready by 2037 with nothing compressed. My concurrence holds on three conditions, checked again at the veto check. (a) No Joint Venture ready date in public, nothing earlier than 2037 for UltraFan NB, and no airframer date. (b) The rationale counts the Joint Venture engine only at the folded programme's bulletin date, or otherwise at 2041. It promises no new combined design (such as P&W's gear in UltraFan) for 2037, because that would compress maturity. (c) The support plan (partner shops on the Singapore model, castings, forgings and gearbox contracts placed in 2035, spares pool and field service in 2036, EIS-readiness review in 2036) is carried as a private other move. If any of these fails, the team rule makes the Civil veto binding. These grounds rest on attributed transcript turns. Solo against Joint Venture is not a Civil ground; that call is the CEO's.

vetoes.plan: Draft public statement ('ready in 2037, seven years from launch'; JV 'on aligned terms', no date)
vetoes.ground: Passes the early-date test: 2037 is 2030 + 7. It gives no Joint Venture ready date, no airframer date, and no 2037 next to NGSA. Not invoked. Adding any of these would be ground (a), and the veto would bind: any UltraFan NB date before 2037, a Joint Venture date, or an airframer's date. Rests on attributed turns.

vetoes.plan: C: `t1000_upgrade: launch` (alone or beside the JV commit)
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It breaks the red line of no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development: 2 years of overlap (2035-37) and $5B of strain. It is -6.02 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.02 / -5.87 against hold, below its own -$2B bill. If it is ordered, I flag a red-line breach for the CEO to strike. Nobody wants those blades more than I do, but in 2045.

vetoes.plan: D: `ultrafan_wb: launch` (alone or beside the JV commit)
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It breaks the overlap red line (beside an UltraFan NB Solo without both being selected), and no Re-engine is on the record to fly it. It is -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.95 in S5 against hold. If it is ordered, I flag a red-line breach for the CEO to strike.

vetoes.plan: E: `ultrafan_nb_solo: cancel` (alone or with the JV)
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground: cancel discipline is the company rule and the CEO's call. As advice, hold. At year 5 of 7 a cancel writes off $5.71B and the test hours already run, and it is -24.54 / -3.22 / -42.25 / -24.54 / -24.54 against hold. NGSA's code 7 still flies it, so the round-1 plan for failure has not triggered and can be retired.

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would invoke the Civil veto, and the team rule makes it binding, in any of these cases: the final statement or a public other move gives any UltraFan NB date before 2037, a Joint Venture ready date or an airframer's date; the Joint Venture terms or the rationale count on a new combined engine (P&W's gear in UltraFan, or a redesigned core) for NGSA's 2037 entry, which would compress maturity; or the rationale drops the support plan (2035 partner-shop and castings, forgings and gearbox contracts, spares pool and field service in 2036, EIS-readiness review in 2036). I would press the zero margin harder, as advice and as a maturity concern for the Board, if gearbox durability evidence is not clean going into the 2036 review. I would move from commit to hold on the Joint Venture if McCabe withholds her co-signature, or if the terms do not keep the folded programme on its own test clock. I would back widebody spend in 2045, upgrade first and only once UltraFan NB is out of development, in any of these cases: a rival-engined Re-engine appears on the record; a further CFM widebody gain eats the 5.2 pp of headroom; or the projection falls below 55%. A named airline win for UltraFan on NGSA would firm up the support build and the ramp.
ops.memo:
Readiness first. UltraFan NB, launched 2030, is ready in 2037: the full seven years. NGSA enters service in 2037: zero margin, a pass with a note, not a veto. Nothing has been cut. Gearbox sizing was a design item in 2030-32 and is closed at design; gearbox durability is what the EIS-readiness review in 2036 has to clear. If a phase slips, the engine slips.

Support. This is the round we contract it: partner shops on our Singapore model, and castings, forgings and gearbox supply with our high-performing suppliers. Spares pool and field service stand up in 2036. Carry that in the rationale and support is in place before EIS. Airbus is locking titanium forgings for its own ramp, so we place ours now.

Joint Venture. Formed this round, the engine takes a folded programme's date, UltraFan 2037 or GTF2 2036, so it is ready by NGSA's entry with nothing compressed, provided the folded programme keeps its own test clock. P&W's gear isn't on offer, and a new gearbox two years from EIS would restart maturity testing. No Joint Venture date in public. I concur on a commit; no Civil veto.

Strain. Nothing widebody until UltraFan is ready: the upgrade is -6.02, UltraFan WB -9.00, both red lines. The upgrade returns in 2045; withdraw the Joint Venture then if unformed.

Capacity. 965 narrowbody engines in 2037, nearly five times our 197 widebody. Partner shops and our best suppliers.

Widebody holds 58%, then 55.2%. We're pacing that programme properly.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney (the jv_with_pw: commit order). The terms: shared risk and investment, and each side's technology protected. Our UltraFan technology is protected the way P&W protects its gear and core. If P&W comes to the table, we form it; if not, UltraFan goes on alone. No ready date and no airframer date are given for any Joint Venture engine [RX-0118, RX-0072, R-1010].

other_moves.move: Joint Venture internal conditions (structure and maturity)
other_moves.detail: (1) RR funds nothing beyond its $4B share and carries none of P&W's costs. (2) If the Joint Venture forms, a folded programme keeps its own test clock and certification path. Internally the Joint Venture engine counts only at that programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, GTF2 2036), and otherwise at formation + 6. (3) No new combined design is offered for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan and no core change. A gearbox change at year 5 of 7 would restart maturity testing. (4) Our support plan carries over unchanged, and we do not count on P&W's shops, because the GTF fleet keeps first call on them [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: 2045 withdrawal review of the standing commitment
other_moves.detail: If the Joint Venture has not formed by the 2045 round, we place a sealed jv_with_pw: withdraw in the 2045 orders, unless that round's grid shows the commit at or above hold. By then NGSA and fps are in service, so no live airframe could use a Joint Venture engine in time, and keeping it would be options management [RX-0051, R-1573]. No widebody item goes beside a standing commitment. The withdrawal goes in the same round as any Trent 1000 upgrade, so the $5B strain cannot come back.

other_moves.move: UltraFan NB test programme held to its seven-year clock
other_moves.detail: Launched 2030, ready 2037, which is year 5 of 7 now. Certification and maturity testing run 2035-37. Gearbox sizing was closed at design in 2030-32. Gearbox durability is the item the EIS-readiness review must clear. That review is in 2036 and stays private, with a final certification gate before the first engine is delivered. If a phase slips, the engine slips. At zero margin we accept not being fitted at entry rather than cut a test [RX-0296, RX-0284].

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support build: 2035 contracting (Watson's plan, step 4 due)
other_moves.detail: Placed in 2035: (a) partner-shop agreements on our Singapore joint-venture model near the launch operators, with no narrowbody MRO scale of our own [RX-0287]; (b) castings, forgings and gearbox supply contracts with high-performing suppliers. Airbus is locking titanium forgings for its own ramp, so ours go now [RX-0286]. Repair technology continues alongside the test programme. The spares pool and field-service team stand up in 2036. The EIS-readiness review is in 2036. Support is in place before entry into service. The plan is resized if Airbus changes its code, and carries over unchanged if the Joint Venture forms. Capacity, as advice: 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes to our best suppliers, not spread thin.

other_moves.move: Round-1 plan for failure retired
other_moves.detail: NGSA still carries code 7, so the cancel trigger has not fired. Holding beats cancelling in every column, S2 included (-3.22). 2035 was the last round for a cancel before readiness. UltraFan NB is held to readiness [R-1573, R-1005].

other_moves.move: UltraFan demonstrator path and technology pull-through continue
other_moves.detail: UltraFan technology continues to feed the Trent fleet for time on wing. Public R&D money is used where available. Qualitative only; it changes no payoff on the grid [RX-0094, RG-0065].

other_moves.move: Trent fleet durability (time on wing) continues as funded
other_moves.detail: About £1bn over four years, separate from UltraFan money [RX-0123, RX-0246]. This is not the t1000_upgrade order, which stays at hold. Qualitative only.

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline
other_moves.detail: No price concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. No payoff on this board.

other_moves.move: Widebody franchise watch for 2045
other_moves.detail: RR widebody share is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, a headroom of 5.2 pp. The franchise test triggers in 2045 on any of three events: a rival-engined Re-engine on the record, a further CFM widebody gain, or a projection below 55%. The Trent 1000 upgrade comes first, once UltraFan NB is out of development: against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium within $3B. UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap [R-1574, RX-0101].

decision.public_statement: So, let me be clear. UltraFan for the narrowbody is in development and on its seven-year clock: ready in 2037, seven years from launch, and not before. The full test programme runs and nothing is compressed. If a phase slips, the engine slips. Support goes in place through partner shops before entry into service. We do not want to underestimate the risks. Partnership has always been our preference, and today we put it on the record: Rolls-Royce commits to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney on aligned terms. That means shared risk and investment, with each side's technology protected. We are actually bringing a technology. If Pratt & Whitney comes to the table, we form it. If not, we deliver on our own. Widebody is our franchise. There is no new widebody engine spend without a Re-engine, and durability work on the Trent fleet goes on. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
So, the decision, by the team rule.

1. START FROM THE PROPOSAL. ultrafan_nb_solo: hold, which keeps the programme to readiness with no cancel. jv_with_pw: commit. ultrafan_wb: hold. t1000_upgrade: hold. Both memos recommend exactly these orders, and the Board says it would approve them.

2. BINDING VETO CHECKS.
- CFO. McCabe co-signs the commit against the hurdle. It is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 against 'UltraFan NB: hold', +0.23 expected, worst column 0, with no new cash in any column. She withholds her signature on the upgrade, on UltraFan WB and on a commit beside either widebody item. None of these is ordered. She invokes no balance-sheet veto. The remaining $2.29B of Solo spend ($8B x 2/7, about $1.14B or £0.84bn a year in 2036-37, £1.68bn in total) comes from free cash flow, after the 2026-28 returns programme and inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. No equity, no borrowing, leverage at or below about 1.5x.
- Civil. Watson invokes no Civil veto. UltraFan NB, ready 2037 (2030 + 7), against NGSA's 2037 EIS is zero margin: a pass with a note. His concurrence rests on three conditions, and all three are met in these orders.
  (a) The public statement gives no UltraFan NB date before 2037, no Joint Venture ready date and no airframer date. 2037 is not placed next to NGSA, and the date is framed as a clock, 'not before'.
  (b) I count the Joint Venture engine only at a folded programme's bulletin date (UltraFan 2037, or GTF2 2036) and otherwise at formation + 6 (2041). I promise no new combined design for 2037: no P&W gear in UltraFan, no core change. The folded programme keeps its own test clock (private other move).
  (c) The support plan is carried as a private other move with its dates. Partner-shop agreements on the Singapore model and the castings, forgings and gearbox contracts are placed in 2035. The spares pool and field service stand up in 2036, and the EIS-readiness review is in 2036.
- No binding veto stands, and overrides is empty.

3. GRID, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5). My weights, which McCabe confirmed: S1 0.55, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05.
- S2 is a signal: Airbus's 2035 code review is on the record.
- S3 and S4 have nothing on the record.
- S5 sits below 'nothing': Boeing has said no second development, and Airbus says the A350 family is its focus.
Item by item:
- JV commit ('hold + commit to JV' minus 'hold'): 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights and on the Board's case (0.55 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.10); +0.11 to +0.46 with S4 at 0.05-0.20. Worst column 0, against a $4B limit. In S4 the whole +2.29 is spend not made: the $1.71B beyond our $4B share is already spent, sunk, with no new cash.
- Trent 1000 upgrade: -6.02 / -6.02 / -6.03 / -6.02 (-6.03 beside the JV) / -5.87. Expected -6.01, worst -6.03. That is beyond its own $2B bill and above the $3B cap, and it is a red line. Not ordered.
- UltraFan WB: -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -9.00 / -6.95. Expected -8.90, worst -9.00. There is no Re-engine on the record, it overlaps UltraFan NB, and it is far above the $1B sub-cap. Not ordered.
- Cancel UltraFan NB: -24.54 / -3.22 / -42.25 / -24.54 / -24.54. Expected -22.05 (-19.99 beside the JV, -4.00 in S4). Worst -42.25. NGSA's code 7 flies it. Not ordered.
Row EVs: 'hold + commit to JV' +15.99; hold +15.76; 'hold + JV + T1000' +9.98; 'hold + T1000' +9.75; 'hold + JV + UltraFan WB' +7.09; 'hold + UltraFan WB' +6.87; 'cancel + JV' -4.00; cancel -6.28.

4. EXPECTED SCENARIO AND BEST PLAN. I expect S1, rivals hold. Its best plan is 'UltraFan NB: hold' at +18.26, tied with 'hold + commit to JV' at +18.26. The commit is best or tied-best in every column and best outright in S4 (+20.55). Premium $0B.

5. OFF-GRID (inference, nothing booked). If S3 and S4 come in the same round, equal shares could hand P&W up to about $8.9B of the fps upside, at a joint weight of about 0.01. If S2 and S4 come together, the Joint Venture keeps us on NGSA and recovers about $10.7B, at a joint weight of about 0.02. Net about +0.12. The two roughly offset, the S2 hedge is the larger, and the sign of +0.23 does not change. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so P&W cannot time its commit to Boeing's or Airbus's code.

6. WHY COMMIT, ON MY RECORD. 'We don't commit that easily' [RX-0124], so I do not take this lightly. The commitment costs nothing in any column, and an airframe can use it: NGSA's live code 7 includes both makers, and a 2035 formation is ready by 2037 from the folded UltraFan. So it is a choice, not options management [RX-0051]. Partnership is the preference, not a need [RX-0118]. The terms credit what we bring [RX-0072]: shared risk and investment, our technology protected as P&W protects its gear and core. It saves the last $2.29B if P&W comes in, which is cash as an input [RX-0042]. The test is binary [RX-0050]: P&W comes to the table, or we deliver alone. It is not open-ended. A sealed withdrawal is planned for 2045 unless that grid shows the commit at or above hold, and no widebody item goes beside it. The thresholds and the Joint Venture terms are doctrine and inference, not my record: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms.

7. RED LINES, CHECKED AGAINST THE FINAL ORDERS.
- No cancel of a flown programme: met.
- No widebody item beside UltraFan NB in development: met. Strain $0.
- jv_with_pw commit: met on the partner test (NGSA's live code 7 includes P&W), co-signed, with no Civil veto and no widebody item beside it.
- No early date and no airframer date: met.
- No item loses more than its own bill: the commit's worst column is 0.
- Premium within cap: $0B.
- No price concessions.
No colleague flagged a red-line breach against these orders. The flags both raised (upgrade, UltraFan WB, cancel) apply to options that are not ordered.

8. CAPACITY AND THE FRANCHISE (advice). Narrowbody volume is 965 engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work goes through partner shops and our best suppliers. Widebody is 58.0% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, so the franchise holds above 50%. The franchise test comes back in 2045.

Remaining Solo spend is about £0.84bn a year, £1.68bn in total, funded from free cash flow with no balance-sheet veto. Her withheld signatures on the upgrade, UltraFan WB and any commit beside a widebody item are binding, and I respect them: none is ordered. I adopt both of her conditions as private other moves: a sealed withdraw in 2045 unless that grid shows the commit at or above hold, and nothing widebody beside a standing commitment. I also adopt her off-grid bound (S3+S4 -0.09 against S2+S4 +0.21) and book nothing from it. On cash, the hurdle and the downside, her test is my evidence.

I take his advice to place forgings contracts now, given Airbus's lock on titanium, and not to count on P&W's shops. recommendations.text: Zero margin at NGSA. UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 against NGSA's 2037 EIS. We want the 2036 EIS-readiness review to clear gearbox durability on test evidence, not on slides. If a phase slips, the engine slips: we accept not being fitted at entry rather than cut a test. Never put a 2036 date on an RR engine in public. Do not move 2037 earlier to answer Airbus's code review. In 2045, Watson should report what the review found and whether RR was fitted at NGSA's entry.

The 2045 withdrawal review. No round falls between 2035 and 2045, so this commitment will stand for ten years. In 2045 the package should show the grid row with `jv_with_pw: withdraw` against the standing commitment. It should place a sealed withdrawal unless that grid shows the commitment at or above hold, and in the same round as any widebody item, so the $5B strain cannot come back through a later formation. Watson flagged that the rules do not say whether an UltraFan that is already ready still folds into a Joint Venture formed later. The ExCo should settle that from the 2045 brief before relying on the commitment.

Joint Venture terms. Keep the private conditions: RR funds nothing beyond its $4B share and carries none of P&W's costs. A folded programme keeps its own test clock. No P&W gear or core change is offered for 2037. Our support plan does not count on P&W's shops. We accept McCabe's off-grid bound on Boeing naming RR (S3) and P&W committing (S4) in the same round, against Airbus dropping us (S2) and P&W committing, and book nothing from either.

Support and capacity. Watson's 2035 contracts (partner shops on the Singapore model; castings, forgings and gearbox supply with high-performing suppliers) should be confirmed as placed, with the spares pool and field service standing up in 2036. Capacity is advice, not a ground: 965 narrowbody engines in 2037 and 990 at the 2039 peak, against 197 widebody a year. Work should go to our best suppliers and partner shops, not be spread thin.

Cash. McCabe should report the remaining Solo spend, about $1.14B (£0.84bn) a year in 2036-37, against a broadly flat R&D envelope and the post-2028 distribution plan, with leverage at or below about 1.5x. If the Joint Venture forms and the £1.68bn is not spent, that saving is not a reason to bring widebody spend beside a standing commitment.

Widebody franchise for 2045. The test does not trigger today: 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, with no Re-engine on the record. In 2045, once UltraFan NB is out of development and the Joint Venture is formed or withdrawn, bring the Trent 1000 upgrade first. That can be against a Re-engine on the record, or as a declared premium inside $3B. UltraFan WB comes only against a Re-engine on the record, within the $1B sub-cap. Watch for a rival-engined Re-engine or a further CFM widebody gain on the 5.2 pp headroom.

Pricing and the public statement. Keep pricing discipline: no concessions to keep NGSA's selection or to win fps. Narrowbody is an option, not a need. In later statements keep 2037 as 'not before', give no Joint Venture ready date, and put nothing beside any airframer's dates.

board_review.note: Product safety is and always must be our most important priority; the balance sheet comes next. This package keeps UltraFan NB to its seven-year clock, holds both widebody items while it is in development, and cancels nothing an airframe flies. The one Board item, the Joint Venture commitment, is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 against hold: +0.23 expected, worst column 0 against a $4B bill. McCabe co-signs it, Watson invokes no Civil veto, and NGSA's code 7 includes Pratt & Whitney. We approve. We do not want to underestimate the risks: zero margin at NGSA's 2037 entry, a support build only now contracted, and a commitment that stands until 2045. We expect gearbox durability cleared at the 2036 review, a sealed withdrawal in 2045 unless that grid supports it, and nothing widebody beside it. With these priorities set, the CEO has our total support.
